Business.title: Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on wide range of US goods
Business.text:
Canada has announced it will impose tariffs on a wide range of key American industries including cosmetics, dairy, wood products and outdoor equipment in the coming weeks, as it retaliates roughly “dollar for dollar” against levies imposed by the US.

In a strong Canadian countermove to tariffs levied by Donald Trump, which took effect on Saturday after trade talks collapsed the day before, Canada’s finance and industry ministers on Tuesday called the measure a “focused response” to what they see as unfair trade practices.

The White House claimed it was using section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to protest against “discriminatory” trade policies by Canada, including provincial bans on US alcohol – a ban that was only implemented in protest against tariffs imposed on Canadian goods last year.

The prime minister, Mark Carney, had previously pledged a “dollar-for-dollar” response from his government after roughly 5% of exports to the US were singled out by the White House.

The retaliatory Canadian measures will cover C$27.6bn ($19.9bn) in imports and are meant to target key industries including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper.

The list from Ottawa has more than 700 items, ranging from from hockey sticks to ornamental fish and toilet paper to smoked lobster, with most of the tariffs set at 25% or 50%. A small group of items, including air conditioning units and tool parts, will face a lower 15% tariff. The levies will be effective starting 8 September and only apply to goods originating from the US.

In announcing the retaliatory measures, the finance minister, François-Philippe Champagne, said the country was united in its fight against the US, telling attenders that Canada remained “masters of our own home”.

The industry minister, Mélanie Joly, called on businesses and consumers to buy Canadian goods as part of a broader “resistance” movement in the trade war.

“You have power,” she said.

The government also announced more than C$7bn in support for businesses affected by the latest tariffs, adding to more than C$20bn in support announced over the past 18 months.

Canada’s decision to retaliate means both countries have doubled down on a trade war that could cost billions.

Earlier on Tuesday, Trump said he was giving “serious consideration” to changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” – reminiscent of his decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Others pointed out that Ontario, Canada’s most populous province, was named after the lake, not the other way around.

Trump’s frustration with Ontario in particular stems from his feud with the province’s premier, Doug Ford, who called the president a “loser” and the “king of bankruptcies” and told the US president to “kiss my ass”. He also threatened to cut electricity and rare earth metal exports to the US.

Trump called Ford a “flunky” of “Governor Carney” and warned “these clowns to ‘fall in line’ or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!”

Trump later alluded to revelations that his trade negotiators had looked to weaken French language rules, saying he would “never interfere” with Canadians speaking French, calling it a “lie … made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister in an attempt to gain political support”.

Trump later added: “I love French Canadians!”

Business.title: US Treasury’s Scott Bessent ‘will lose’ battle with bond markets, former mentor warns
Business.text:
Scott Bessent’s attempt to calm the bond markets and push down America’s cost of borrowing have attracted a rebuke from the US Treasury secretary’s former mentor.

The billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller, who worked with Bessent at George Soros’s fund management firm in the 1990s, has warned that his former pupil is courting danger by trying to suppress US bond yields.

Druckenmiller, writing in the Wall Street Journal, argued that the US should “let the bond market speak”, rather than expand its bond purchases in an effort to push up prices, and lower borrowing costs.

“Governments defending prices against fundamentals always lose. The only variable is how much they spend before conceding,” he wrote.

Druckenmiller argued that Washington should heed the rise in borrowing costs – measured by bond yields – and take steps to cut the budget deficit, rather than interfering in the market to push yields down again.

“The long-term Treasury yield is the most important price in the world. It is also the only fiscal disciplinarian the US has left. Neither party will run on entitlement reform. Both have spent the past decade expanding commitments while ignoring arithmetic,” he wrote.

Druckenmiller’s intervention comes after Bessent decided to at least double the maximum size of the Treasury’s buyback operations, from $2bn (£1.5bn) to $4bn. That move briefly led to a drop in US long-term bond yields, but this quickly reversed.

“The market’s verdict was swift and correct: This wasn’t liquidity management, it was price management – and a mistake far larger than $4bn suggests,” Druckenmiller said.

Bond yields fall when prices rise, and vice versa.

Yesterday, CNBC reported that Bessent could increase his bond-buying firepower by conducting purchases using the Treasury’s near-$1tn General Account, a government fund held at the Federal Reserve.

Last week the US national debt hit $40tn, and rising, and the annual deficit is expected to hit $2tn this year.

Addressing this primary deficit is the “only thing that durably lowers long-term yields”, Druckenmiller wrote in the WSJ.

“The reward is enormous: A credible fiscal package would do more for the long end of the curve than a buyback program 1,000 times this size,” he said.

Bessent’s bond market intervention is a signal that “Washington is increasingly uncomfortable with soaring long-term borrowing costs,” said Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG.

Bessent’s attempts to battle the financial markets are ironic, as he worked alongside Soros when he beat the Bank of England and forced the pound to crash out of the European exchange rate mechanism in 1992.

That drama, which became known as Black Wednesday, showed how hard it is for a government to defend a currency when investors believe it is overvalued.

But despite that experience, Bessent took part in a joint operation with Japan to prop up the yen earlier this month – seemingly to prevent Tokyo selling US bonds to fund yen purchases.

“The irony of the guy working for Soros and Druckenmiller who broke the Bank of England back in 1992 pretending that you can do FX intervention alone, and lastingly defend a currency, is just amazing,” Adam Posen, the president of the Peterson Institute and an expert on the Japanese economy, told the Financial Times earlier this month.

Rising geopolitical tensions have pushed bond yields higher, as the failure of the US-Iran peace talks lifted the oil price – which threatens to drive inflation higher.

The collapse of US-Canada trade talks last weekend has also put foreign policy back in the spotlight, weakening the Canadian dollar. A North American trade war could hurt US growth, creating more fiscal pressure.

Business.title: New York business group sues Mamdani over city-owned grocery stores plan
Business.text:
A New York City business group sued mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday over his plan to create five municipally owned grocery stores.

The Multicultural Business Coalition, which says it represents hundreds of small supermarkets, filed two lawsuits in New York county supreme court on Monday, arguing that the plan violates the civil rights of smaller, immigrant- and minority-owned businesses. The group argues that smaller stores would be unable to match the discounts offered by the city grocery stores and “therefore, will be put out of business,” according to the lawsuits.

During his campaign, which focused heavily on the issue of affordability, Mamdani proposed introducing city-owned, subsidized grocery stores, which he said would help combat rising food costs.

The city plans to open five stores by 2029, with one in each borough. Mamdani has said that plans call for the stores to offer some produce, meat and seafood pantry staples, dairy and other refrigerated goods at prices 30% below typical retail prices – and he has said that the program is projected to cut New Yorkers’ “average grocery bill by 15%”.

The first store is scheduled to open in the Bronx in 2027.

The first lawsuit filed on Monday against Mamdani’s plan argues that the city did not conduct any “serious analysis” of how the new stores could affect smaller neighborhood grocers before launching the initiative. The second, meanwhile, argues that the city does not have the legal authority to create the stores.

Speaking to CNN on Monday, attorney Mark Jaffe, general counsel for the Multicultural Business Coalition and president of the Greater New York Chamber of Commerce, said: “You cannot expect hard-working small business owners to compete with a supermarket that isn’t going to pay rent, won’t have to pay an electric bill and won’t have to buy their products at full price.”

He added: “They cannot possibly compete because no one will be subsidizing them.”

Mamdani defended the plan at a news conference on Monday, where he was asked about the lawsuits.

“I continue to be fully confident in both the legality and the importance of our initiative to deliver five city-run grocery stores, one in each borough, to the people of our city,” he said. “We are talking about a reflection of a cost of living crisis that has seen grocery prices increase by about 30% over the last few years, and we’re also talking about delivering five city-run grocery stores in a city of 8.5 million people that has more than a thousand grocery stores.”

He also said the city has subsidized groceries on Essex Street in Manhattan and Moore Street in Brooklyn. And he argued that they have “not had a negative effect on bodegas around them or on grocery stores around them”.

New York City’s Economic Development Corporation (EDC), which is overseeing the stores, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuits on Tuesday.

But, a spokesperson for the EDC told the New York Times on Monday that the city was “evaluating programs and policies to support local grocers”.

“We are looking at the potential for tax abatement, incentives and zoning benefits through existing city programs to ensure that the city is doing everything in our power to alleviate cost pressures for small businesses across the city,” the spokesperson added.

Sports.title: Honest Ahanor: Chelsea in talks to sign Atalanta and Italy defender
Sports.text:
Chelsea are in talks to sign Atalanta defender Honest Ahanor.

The Blues expressed an interest in the 18-year-old Italian when they signed right-back Marco Palestra from the Serie A side in July.

BBC Sport has been told Atalanta are willing to sell Ahanor if their 40m euro (£34.3m) valuation is met.

Ahanor, who mainly plays at left-back, joined Atalanta from Genoa on a three-year deal last summer for a reported fee of 16m euros, plus 4m euros in add-ons.

He made 28 appearances in Serie A for Atalanta last season, establishing himself as a regular starter for the Italian club. He also made his Champions League debut in a 2-1 win against Club Brugge in September.

In May, he was called up by Italy for friendly matches against Luxembourg and Greece.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has been building his squad since taking over at Stamford Bridge in July, signing England midfielder Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa for a club record £117m, and adding experienced Premier League players Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson.

Sports.title: Nico Gonzalez: 'Mini Rodri' shown he will be loved at Newcastle
Sports.text:
Nico Gonzalez wanted to feel loved. He quickly got his wish at St James' Park on Wednesday night after completing his £52m move from Manchester City.

Newcastle United's new signing was handed a rapturous welcome before he even kicked a ball for the club as supporters repeatedly chanted his name.

The sight of Gonzalez walking out at the sold-out stadium before the 3-2 win against West Bromwich Albion in the Carabao Cup second round was a welcome one for head coach Matthias Jaissle, who desperately wanted him.

The German stressed he was "always a believer in the positive things", but tellingly also referred to the pursuit as a "long fight".

Having spoken personally to Gonzalez on a number of occasions, Jaissle made it clear how much he wanted the 24-year-old and how pivotal he would be in his side.

That stuck with him.

"It's always important if you're making signings like Nico that there is a commitment there," Jaissle said.

"But he showed that from the beginning, from our first conversations."

A lot has clearly changed since Gonzalez first set foot in the Premier League a year and a half ago and made his Manchester City debut against Newcastle. Of all teams.

Before City's 4-0 win, the new arrival had been warned about the intensity Newcastle's midfielders played and pressed with at their snarling best.

But the unfazed Spaniard ended up completing a staggering 100 passes, and helped snuff out any potential breakaways from the visitors at Etihad Stadium.

It was a glimpse of the skillset - in and out of possession - which convinced Manchester City to sign defensive midfielder Gonzalez from Porto for £50m.

City's then manager, Pep Guardiola, even labelled him "our mini-Rodri" in the absence of his influential, injured team-mate.

Gonzalez ultimately found an extended run of starts hard to come by once his compatriot returned to full fitness, though.

But former Manchester City assistant manager Kolo Toure believes he will have benefited from his experience at the Etihad.

"When you are in competition against players like Rodri, you learn a lot because you come up against them in training and you have to show the manager you are better than them," he said.

"You learn from things they do as well and, on the ball, he learned a lot from Rodri. Without the ball he's really good because he can press, get it back and read the game really well.

"He has this capacity to steal the ball from opponents, which is top. He's better than Rodri at this in my opinion, but Rodri on the ball is the best in the world.

"Both of them have different qualities and different strengths."

Gonzalez had a close relationship with Rodri and long humbly recognised that only a select number of players can start in his position at clubs bidding to challenge for the biggest honours.

Rodri was that man at Manchester City under Guardiola and, following the midfielder's move to Barcelona, new manager Enzo Maresca has signed Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille, having already brought in Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest.

The club also look set to make a bid for Chelsea's Enzo Fernandez.

It was still not easy for Gonzalez to leave Manchester City, where he felt settled, but Newcastle will give him the platform he has been longing for as a key player.

The enthusiastic Spaniard sees this as an opportunity to develop further, which has always been a driver.

"His mentality is top," Toure said. "I would review games individually with the players and every time I had my laptop and sat next to him, he was so open to learning.

"He wanted me to show him and I wanted to help him because he was demanding in that way.

"You want to have players like this because they want to see what they do well and not well, and are open to criticism.

"He's going to keep on improving because of his mentality."

Gonzalez certainly did so when he left Barcelona, where his professional career started, and has such experience to fall back on.

Having spent a decade at Barca, and risen through the ranks, Gonzalez ultimately had to depart to truly flourish elsewhere.

Following a successful loan spell at Valencia, he joined Porto on a permanent basis at the age of 21 before earning a move to Manchester City.

Former Barcelona B team-mate Roger Riera feels he has developed "another vision" as a result.

"Nico has seen different countries and different styles of football," he said. "He's added a lot of things to his game, which have made him a more complete player.

"He is a better package now."

Sports.title: England v Pakistan: Joe Root shows himself to be the leader England need
Sports.text:
At the back of the Compton Stand at Lord's is an enormous picture of Ben Stokes.

In the snap, Stokes unleashes a bouncer to a flinching Mohammed Siraj, the India tailender. It was taken during England's heart-stopping 22-run win on this ground last summer.

England's defeat of India was all about Stokes. He made contributions with the bat in both innings, ran out Rishabh Pant with a direct hit and put in a trademark marathon bowling spell on the final day. Stokes came to the post-match media conference with blood seeping through his sock.

Throughout Stokes' tenure as England captain, the question loomed of how anyone would eventually go about succeeding him.

For better or worse, Stokes became the all-encompassing figure in the team, for his performances on the field and what he said or did off it. It was hard to imagine how anyone could emerge from his shadow without having their leadership compared to the talismanic all-rounder.

England are little more than a week into the post-Stokes era and there is already no doubt about the strength of leadership at the helm. This is Joe Root's team now.

The last thing Root would have wanted at the beginning of his second reign as skipper was the Brydon Carse controversy.

Yet, the Yorkshireman has shown himself to be the captain English cricket needs, yet probably does not deserve.

Root's measured, assured and honest address to the media at Lord's on Tuesday was the most impressive display of leadership from anyone connected with the England team in a long time.

Perhaps Root is helped by the circumstances. If Brendon McCullum was still around, he would have been pushed in front of cameras, but McCullum has gone and his replacement Stephen Fleming is yet to arrive. It leaves Root as unquestionably the man in charge.

In terms of Root's second coming as skipper, the off-field part might be the easy bit. It is on the field where he now has a point to prove.

He said as much last week before the Headingley Test - that the biggest challenge in resuming the captaincy was overcoming the perceptions others have of his leadership.

It is not that Root was an awful captain first time around - far from it. It is just the abiding memory is an awful ending of only one win from 17 matches, a horror run that left Root and his team broken.

Leeds was a dream restart, an innings win over Pakistan wrapped up inside three days.

But the one-sided nature of that victory did not give Root room to show what kind of on-field captain he will be this time around. His best act at Headingley was to win the toss and, after Ollie Robinson took a wicket with the first ball of the match, England were on top.

There have been glimpses of what the New Root could become.

Stokes' preference for naming an England team two days before a Test has gone, at least for now. England are likely to be unchanged at Lord's, though that will not be confirmed until the toss.

Root has removed himself from first slip and now fields at mid-off. It may only be a temporary move, but it puts him closer to his bowlers. On the first morning at Headingley, Root yanked a wayward Jofra Archer from the attack after only two overs. It is hard to imagine he would have done the same to either Stuart Broad or James Anderson.

There was a hint of funkiness in the field, albeit an overhang from Root's first spell as captain. The dismissal of Azan Awais in Pakistan's second innings was the eighth time a seamer under Root has had a catch taken at leg slip - the most of any captain since such data began being collected in 2006.

Asked what the difference was between the captaincy of Stokes and Root, fast bowler Josh Tongue said: "It's very chilled out there." Tongue probably did not mean to imply Root brings a greater calmness than Stokes, yet few would argue he has taken the intensity down a notch or two.

For all the impressive media conferences, bowling changes and leg slips, Root will be judged on results, and a win this week would give England their first series triumph since 2024.

There will be plenty of attention on the Lord's pitch, so heavily criticised after England's win against New Zealand. On Wednesday, Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC) chairman Mark Nicholas and director of cricket Rob Lynch were seen taking a good look at the surface.

Pakistan should be better than their showing at Headingley, mainly because they cannot get much worse. They are boosted by the return of captain Babar Azam from a hand injury and have won the previous two Tests they have played here.

England will want to build on the green shoots of recovery that sprouted in Leeds.

Jordan Cox impressed at number three and is highly rated by the management. There could be a logjam in the top order when Jacob Bethell returns to fitness, so all of Cox, Emilio Gay, Dan Lawrence and Jamie Smith will want to ensure they are not squeezed out.

Root said his quartet of fast bowlers "do not know how good they can be". That foursome now have the opportunity to show they can be England's first-choice attack in a range of conditions. It is a bad time for Carse to put himself out of the picture.

As for Root, no man has more runs or hundreds on this ground. Now he returns as the captain, already leading by example this week.

"When you have the privilege of being a leader within a team, you want to build something bigger than just winning," he said. "I feel like I didn't do that very well first time around.

"There's a lot to look forward to, there's a lot to work hard towards. I guess that's the fun side of it."

For Root and his players, following the past few days, the fun side will simply be returning to playing cricket.

Sports.title: Ander Herrera: Why midfielder is playing for free at Real Zaragoza
Sports.text:
Ander Herrera's most recent competitive game was in front of a raucous La Bombonera crowd playing for Boca Juniors in the Copa Libertadores.

His next will be in the Spanish third division in front of roughly 6,500 fans against a regional side, Gimnastic de Tarragona.

But Herrera says his return to Real Zaragoza on a free transfer from Boca is just as important as any move he has made in his career.

"This is probably the last dream that I wanted to make come true," the Spaniard tells BBC Sport.

"To come back home, to the place where I grew up, that gave me the opportunity to be professional - not only in football, also as a human being.

"And I still have the passion, I still have the desire. I still have that love for football and to do it at home is the best way to end up in my career.

"In Spain, we say closing the circle."

The midfielder has returned to his boyhood club after 15 years away - including two spells at Athletic Club and stints at Manchester United, Paris St-Germain and Boca.

The 37-year-old has won the Europa League, FA Cup and multiple league titles, played under Jose Mourinho, Thomas Tuchel and Marcelo Bielsa, and shared dressing rooms with Lionel Messi, Neymar and Wayne Rooney.

However, success has been in short supply in recent years for Zaragoza, who beat Arsenal in the 1995 Cup Winners' Cup final.

They were relegated from La Liga in 2012-13 - two years after Herrera had left for Bilbao - and after 13 seasons of declining finishes in the second division, fell into the notoriously difficult third tier of Spanish football.

"It has been so sad, of course, for all us Zaragozistas," says Herrera, who watched the club's decline from afar.

"Real Zaragoza belong to Europe, they belong to compete for trophies, to be fighting with the biggest clubs in Spain and in Europe.

"I want to put my quality, my experience and my passion to try to help my team to come back where I think we belong.

"But since the first day I came, I don't want to talk too much about the past. We have been talking too much about what we have done wrong.

"It's always killing our minds why that happened, always thinking about negative things. Let's stop crying about what happened in the past.

"Let's build on the future. Let's come every day to training with a smile."

When Herrera left Zaragoza, who were in financial trouble, in 2011, he knew he wanted to return at some point.

While he did not know what the situation for his comeback would be, he has rejoined the club during their most challenging time - and opted to donate his salary to Zaragoza's foundation.

"I don't need a contract. I have a very successful career. I have taken care of my money," Herrera says.

"I can give this present to myself. To put that shirt on... for free because I wanted to help my club, my team, my city.

"It's something that I wanted to do. It's something that I am able to do and it's something that makes me feel so proud to be able to be here just to help.

"I am not thinking about money or contracts. I feel a privilege to be able to do that."

Herrera was a fervent fan before his promotion to Zaragoza's squad. His idols were from the club and his biggest inspiration - his father Pedro - was also a player before becoming general manager.

Herrera Sr's time working at Zaragoza was when his son's earliest football memories were created, including that famous 1995 European success.

The young Ander watched from home as his team beat Arsenal to clinch the trophy in the Parc des Princes, the home of PSG - a club he later spent three years at.

Herrera says: "You can now see the difference between Arsenal and Real Zaragoza - but we used to fight against those giants."

Herrera's on-pitch peak may be behind him - although he remains focused on short-term objectives such as helping rebuild Zaragoza - but he is sure football will remain part of his future after his playing days are over.

"I like to work with young players," he says. "I like to see the development and the process and I like to help them to avoid some mistakes that I have probably made.

"To help the families also manage situations that I have already managed in the past and I have probably done not as good as I should have done.

"I don't know if I'm going to be a coach of professional football players. I don't close any door because I love football, it's my passion, it's something that I have been doing my whole life and it's something that I love.

"But I don't know in which position I will find my place."

As Herrera's career progressed and he became a senior player in dressing rooms, he saw the effect social media can have on younger players.

"Young players want to run too fast and I think if you make two steps instead of one you can make a mistake," says Herrera.

"When I was in Zaragoza's academy I was one of the best players and I had the opportunity to leave, but I didn't want to leave.

"I have always tried to enjoy every single step that I make in my career and you can see in our academy we are having problems to keep the players.

"But we have stats here that most of the players that leave don't reach professional football and the players that stay have more possibilities to reach it.

"So because you run faster, it doesn't mean you are going to reach the objective faster. Social media is making you run too much.

"Every player has his moment. Just because he's doing it faster than you [it doesn't mean] that he's going to be a better player than you.

"Social media is making us live too fast in every aspect of society."

These are messages that Herrera wants to help pass on to a younger generation, either as a coach or in another role.

But if he does choose to become the former, he has a long, and expanding, list of coaches from the Basque Country to look at for inspiration.

Four current Premier League bosses - Xabi Alonso at Chelsea, Mikel Arteta at Arsenal, Aston Villa's Unai Emery and Liverpool's Andoni Iraola - all come from the northern region in Spain and have had established coaching careers.

Herrera, who was born in Bilbao, adds: "I don't know how to explain it. I think it goes in the DNA.

"The capacity to work, the capacity to respect the sport, to make every step and try to be better every day.

"It's difficult to explain this level of Basque coaches, but I think it is the respect for football that you can see in the Basque Country.

"People will never hear a Basque person saying that something in Madrid is better than in the Basque Country and you can replicate that in football.

"They have so much love for their own things and it's something very special to experience."

But Herrera's future coaching ambitions are on hold.

The club he loves are languishing in the third division of Spanish football - and one thing is on his mind.

"I am so proud and I feel so privileged to do every single step that I have made in my career. Hopefully I can end up successful at home."

Sports.title: US Open 2026 qualifying results: Heather Watson to face Harriet Dart for main-draw spot
Sports.text:
Heather Watson and Harriet Dart will go head-to-head for a place in the US Open main draw as six British players made it through to the third and final qualifying round in New York.

Watson kept alive her hopes of a first US Open singles main-draw appearance in five years by overcoming Spain's Angela Fita Boluda in a rollercoaster encounter lasting nearly three hours.

The 34-year-old was twice a break up in the third set and served for the match - only to be taken to a deciding 10-point tie-break.

However, she held her nerve to seal a 6-4 5-7 7-6 (10-5) win.

That set up a meeting with her frequent doubles partner Dart, who beat American 16-year-old Kristina Penickova 5-7 6-0 6-3.

I've not played much in general in the last year and I've had some niggles here and there," Watson told BBC Sport.

"It's been tough with the scheduling as well, there's not been many options - especially when you get old in tennis, you can't do these long-haul flights for a week and then come back.

"It means a lot and I'm very pleased to get through today."

Francesca Jones could also join British number one Katie Boulter in the women's main draw after beating German Mona Barthel 7-6 (7-3) 1-6 6-2 to set up a meeting with Taiwanese player Joanna Garland.

In the men's event, Jacob Fearnley, Toby Samuel and Harry Wendelken are all one win away from joining Cameron Norrie, Arthur Fery and Jan Choinski in the main draw, which begins on Sunday.

Fearnley showed great resilience to battle to victory over Frenchman Luka Pavlovic, which set up a meeting with Austria's Jurij Rodionov.

The 25-year-old world number 100 recovered from a break of serve down to take the opening set, and held his nerve in the decider to clinch a 6-4 6-7 (4-7) 6-4 win.

Samuel, bidding to qualify for the US Open for the first time, produced a 4-6 6-4 6-1 victory against fellow Briton Billy Harris.

The 23-year-old, who made his slam debut at this year's French Open, will face Chile's former top-20 player Cristian Garin next.

Wendelken, who has never contested the main draw at an overseas major, saved a match point to come through a three-hour tussle with Switzerland's Remy Bertola.

The 24-year-old, ranked 196th, appeared on the brink of elimination at a set and 5-2 down but eventually clinched a 5-7 7-6 (7-4) 6-4 win. He will face Lithuania's Vilius Gaubas.

However, Katie Swan and Jack Pinnington Jones both missed out.

Swan fell to American Mary Stoiana 6-7 (5-7) 6-3 6-3, while Pinnington Jones lost 2-6 7-6 (8-6) 6-3 to Finland's Otto Virtanen.

Former semi-finalist Grigor Dimitrov will face Virtanen after the 35-year-old maintained his bid for a 15th US Open men's singles appearance with a 7-6 (7-5) 6-4 win over Kazakhstan's Timofey Skatov.

China's Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen, contesting a Grand Slam qualifying event for the first time since 2022, beat France's Clara Burel won 6-1 7-5 to set up a match against Russian Elena Pridankina.

There was also victory for 2019 US Open champion Bianca Andreescu, who will aim to secure a first US Open main draw appearance in two years against Slovenian Tamara Zidansek after defeating Ukraine's Veronika Podre 6-0 6-3.

Fery, meanwhile, continued his US Open preparations by reaching the quarter-finals at the Winston-Salem Open.

The fourth seed beat Dutch qualifier Mees Rottgering 6-3 6-3 to reach the last eight.

Fery is competing in only his second event since his stunning run to the Wimbledon semi-finals in July.

He will face American Aleksandar Kovacevic for a place in the semi-finals.

Sports.title: Champions League 2026-27: When is the league phase draw and who is in each pot?
Sports.text:
The league phase draw for the 2026-27 Champions League campaign takes place on Thursday, 27 August at 17:00 BST in Monaco.

A total of 36 teams will enter that stage of the competition and while 29 teams qualified at the end of last season, the remaining seven places were decided by play-offs.

In the league phase, each team will face eight different teams once, with four home matches and four away matches.

For the draw, the 36 teams will be placed into four pots with one being the highest-ranked and four being the lowest. The pot placements are based on the club's Uefa club coefficient ranking from the five-season period ending at the conclusion of 2025-26.

Each team will face two teams from each of the four pots and cannot face a team from the same country as themselves.

Uefa announced a new rule on Wednesday that sides cannot host the same team in three successive league phases - so Liverpool will not draw Real Madrid at home and Arsenal will not travel to Inter Milan. Those fixtures could be drawn in reverse though.

The teams who finish in the top eight will qualify for the Champions League's round of 16. Those between ninth and 24th will enter the play-off knockout round. The 12 teams ranked between 25th and 36th will exit the competition when the league phase is concluded.

Sports.title: Wouter Vrancken's side come of age as Hearts bid goodnight Rapid Vienna
Sports.text:
If 16 May was the day the dream ended, 26 August may well turn out to be when the next one started for Hearts.

A mere three months on from a final-day defeat that denied Hearts a first Scottish top-flight title in 66 years, they have not only secured a tangible reward for finishing as runners-up, they did so with immense courage and togetherness.

Thursday's victory over Rapid Vienna on penalties secured a place in Friday's league phase draw for the Conference League and two games each in October, November and December.

A lot has changed in that three months - a new head coach in Belgian Wouter Vrancken, player departures and plenty arrivals - and a sticky start to the season threatened to prolong a sense of malaise after that 3-1 defeat by champions Celtic.

European and domestic losses got the 2026-27 campaign off to a whimper but Vrancken stayed calm and believes his team are now reaping deserved benefits.

"They have to learn that they're a good team, that they're good players, that they can show it," he told BBC Scotland.

"In the last away games in Europe, you see that they're a little bit scared to do things, to take risks or to give spaces away. Then we don't play our game.

"The development of the team, the progress of the team is amazing. The team spirit, I saw it from the first session already.

"They want to learn it. They wanted to have feedback. They want to go into it and the kind of football we played. This is the result. They get rewarded and I'm so happy for them."

While the margin of Hearts' 6-0 aggregate loss to Sturm Graz in the Champions League second qualifying round may have been unexpected, the result was not much of a surprise.

Even less surprising was losing to Benfica, typically a Champions League team, in the Europa League qualifiers, though again the margin was heavy at 7-1 on aggregate.

Facing Rapid Vienna in the Conference League play-off represented another tough tie, though not considered as tough as either Sturm Graz or Benfica.

Roughly this time last year, Dundee United took Rapid to penalties in their Conference League qualifying tie but lost in the shootout and the improvement in Hearts' domestic form after a losing start at Aberdeen raised hopes that European league phase football was achievable.

Hearts more than gave as good as they got in the first leg, but the absence of a lead to take over to Austria made Rapid slight favourites at 2-2, more so after Ercan Kara gave them a 1-0 lead on the night at the Allianz Stadion.

A Tomas Magnusson red card for Hearts preceded the Pierre Landry Kabore equaliser that forced extra time. Calvin Miller's volley very nearly secured them the win only for Nenad Cvetkovic to level for Rapid on 119 minutes.

A first save in the shootout from Beau Reus to deny Moulaye Haidara put Hearts within touching distance again but Oisin McEntee's spot-kick getting blocked prolonged the tension.

Up stepped Marco Tilio, a former Celtic winger perhaps with a point to prove after a frustrating spell in Glasgow. But it was Reus who had the last word with another terrific stop to secure a 4-3 win on penalties.

Vrancken's post-match comments revealed how much he believes his side have come in a short space of time.

"When you see the game, we played a really bad first half, a little bit similar as we did in Benfica," he explained.

"We made agreements, we had a game plan and we didn't follow up, we didn't show the guts to follow up.

"When you play against a side like Rapid Vienna, when you don't show it, they can play through you. We were already pretty angry at half-time and we came out, we did much better.

"We took the game in our hands, we were dominant at that moment. This is already a mental strength, coming back on 1-0 down and coming back like this.

"Again, in the extra time, you try to take the game with you to Hearts and to Edinburgh, then you get a mental kick again in the last minute of the extra time.

"Again, I'm so proud of these guys that they stay in the game, focused and concentrated to win the penalties.

"We can make more steps in the coming weeks and hope that we can take the steps as soon as possible."

Progress in Europe brings obvious financial rewards and there may be sales as well as purchases at Hearts in the closing days of the transfer window.

Hearts have already brought in 12 new players this summer while even more than that have moved on.

Now with at least six more European fixtures to play this season, former Hearts player Ryan Stevenson believes the club will have to recruit.

"I think they'll definitely need to bring in another two or three anyway when you look at the League Cup, the six games in Europe, the league, which is so important," he told BBC Radio Scotland's Sportsound.

Another former Tynecastle favourite, Allan Preston, believes Hearts will be prepared for such a task.

"They've got people ready to come if they're needed," he said. "They are ready. They don't wait until things happen. They already do things.

"If they need to, they'll be pushing the button before the transfer window closes. They will get better, they'll produce better."

One position Hearts may have to look at as a priority is midfield after Tom Renaud's first-half injury.

"That's the biggest disappointment of the evening," lamented Vrancken.

"It's not looking good but I hope for him that it's OK. We have to look there because he was also really good in the last game.

"We're talking every day about those things and we'll see in the next weeks."

Sports.title: Audrey Werro: World record in sights as European champion competes at Diamond League Zurich
Sports.text:
European 800m champion Audrey Werro has backed herself to overhaul one of athletics' oldest and most controversial world records.

Jarmila Kratochvilova, representing the then Czechoslovakia, clocked one minute 53.28 seconds in 1983 and the mark has remained untouched in the 43 years since.

While a systematic doping programme of athletes was in place in the country during her career, Kratochvilova never failed a doping test and has denied cheating., external

Werro, still only 22, ran 1:53.80 in Paris in June, moving up to third in the event's all-time list and to within half a second of Kratochvilova's time.

"Things have happened really fast," said Werro, on the eve of Thursday evening's Diamond League meeting in Zurich.

"I was not prepared for a world record this year. I just want to focus on running fast and winning some races and I think with this mentality the world record will fall one day. But I don't know when."

Werro, a multiple title-winner at youth level, has improved her personal best in each of her last eight seasons and is now consistently within range of the world record.

This year the Swiss has registered three of the 10 fastest times in history.

"The biggest difference this year was that I finished university one year ago," said Werro, who saw off Britain's Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson to claim her continental title in Birmingham earlier this month.

"Now I'm just focused on athletics and I just have more time for the competition, the training, the recovery, everything.

"I have worked a lot more in the mentality part over the past two years and you are seeing the result now."

Werro's trademark celebration, in which she mimics outstretched claws, is in honour of her father's advice to channel the spirit of a lion on the track after her judged her too timid in childhood races.

Sports.title: Tour Championship: Alex Fitzpatrick on leaving Matt's shadow
Sports.text:
If Alex Fitzpatrick wanted a glimpse into just how life changing winning on the PGA Tour would be, he did not have to wait long.

While celebrating victory at the Zurich Classic pairs event, in tandem with his older brother and world number four Matt, at a golf club just north of Palm Beach in Florida, Alex felt a congratulatory hand on his shoulder.

"I look over and it's Michael Jordan," Fitzpatrick says. "I'm like 'wow', it's insane.

"He walks past the table. He's got a bag full of cigars, t-shirt untucked, he looks like the coolest person ever.

"He walked past me, saw Gary Woodland, who won the previous week, and was like 'wow, it's a room of winners in here'. That was the coolest thing ever.

"When I started to really love basketball, I watched videos of him. I love his shoes. I loved everything about him. It was surreal having that moment.

"I'm not someone who gets starstruck but Michael Jordan, having him say stuff to me, it was a different world."

It is a world, though, where Fitzpatrick is looking very much at home.

In addition to his maiden DP World Tour win at the Indian Open in March, Fitzpatrick has five top-10 finishes in 13 starts on the PGA Tour.

While cynics were questioning the merit of receiving a two-year tour card as a result of winning April's Zurich Classic, 2026 has seen Fitzpatrick prove his place alongside the world's best.

And so sure is he of his spot among the elite, Fitzpatrick hasn't actually leaned much on 2022 US Open champion Matt for advice.

"The truth is, we haven't spoken that much about a lot of stuff. I've picked his brain once this year, maybe twice," he says.

"I feel comfortable out here and comfortable around the group of people playing on this tour.

"I've been doing this a long time, I've been playing golf since I was four.

"I haven't asked him a lot of questions about how things work, maybe how to get better with certain things.

"He's always someone I can text or call but he's still my brother and that's more important than the golf side."

When Netflix featured Alex in season two of its fly-on-the-wall documentary Full Swing, the episode was titled 'In The Shadows', and, whether on request of the production crew or not, he introduced himself as "Matt Fitzpatrick's brother" first, then "professional golfer".

This season, the younger Fitzpatrick has been carving his own path.

He followed up the Indian Open and Zurich Classic successes by finishing tied for ninth at the Cadillac Championship in May. He was then fourth at the Truist Championship at Quail Hollow and it was at that tournament in North Carolina when he felt like he belonged at this level.

"I've always had the self belief that I could compete against the best players, but I never had the chance or facts to back up my own belief," he says.

"It was nice to feel like I'm out here for a good reason. At that point, I was confident in my game and at that point I felt I could carry on."

He says his remarkable rise from outside the world's top 250 to number 68 in just 12 months was "kick-started" by working with Matt's former coach Mike Walker on a more permanent basis.

Fitzpatrick adds that "backing himself" was his best decision but does he feel like he has finally forged his own standing in the game?

"I have my own identity," he says. "This year I've really worked on what I want to achieve and who I am as a person.

"That's the big step I've taken. The success on the course doesn't define me."

Sports.title: Muchová and Menšík win $1m US Open mixed doubles title in late-night thriller
Sports.text:
To many who came to the US Open grounds this week, the showpiece of the mixed doubles championship came Tuesday afternoon, with the returns of Serena Williams (after four years away from tennis) and Carlos Alcaraz (after four months out with a wrist injury).

To the players who remained in the field after Williams and Alcaraz exited in the quarter-finals, the real highlight was Wednesday night’s final at Arthur Ashe Stadium, with its $1m in prize money on the line. Karolína Muchová and Jakub Menšík made the most of the spotlight, beating Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli 6-3, 1-6 (10-6) for the title.

Their win capped an event that, in a reversal of recent years, was dominated by singles players instead of doubles specialists. The Czech duo beat Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev 5-4 (8-6) 3-5 (11-9) and the runners-up bested Elina Svitolina and Gael Monfils 4-5 (7-9) 4-1 (10-5) in a pair of competitive semi-finals that each lasted over an hour, making for a final that finished just before midnight.

“This format of a tournament, it went really quickly,” said Muchová, who was playing her first matches since losing the Wimbledon final in June. “I’m obviously super happy that we managed to win. It was not my expectation.”

Since its format was reimagined last year in an effort to entice the top singles players to participate, the mixed doubles competition has drawn criticism. The revamp moved the tournament a week before the start of singles play and raised the winners’ prize from $200,000 to $1m, but cut the field to 16 and drew outcry from doubles specialists kept out of the draw. The 2025 champions, Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori, were specialists, but some questioned whether the new event - with its four-game sets until the final, no ad-scoring and a 10-point tiebreak - should even be categorized as a grand slam title.

Tournament organizers responded this year, adjusting the format to include an eight-team qualifying draw that allowed more specialists to enter. They gathered a captivating field, headlined by Williams playing in New York for the first time since the 2022 match that was her presumptive farewell. Even so, by Tuesday’s end, the tournament had lost not just its highest-profile names - Novak Djokovic and Aryna Sabalenka and Felix Auger-Aliassime and Alex Eala made quick first-round exits - but also its doubles specialist teams, all four of whom were out by the quarter-finals.

What the semi-finalist pairs lacked in spectacle or doubles pedigree, they made up for in another category: bringing the fun that this format encouraged. Asked how they’d spend the time before the final, Bencic answered “beer”, earning a laugh and slight panic from Cobolli. Muchová and Menšík played their matches in color-coordinated pink-and-maroon looks; when Muchová first floated the idea for their outfits, Menšík had to ask what maroon was. Andreeva joked she used to have a crush on the nine-years-older Rublev.

As for Monfils and Svitolina, few pairs in the sport know each other better: they married in 2021 and have a three-year-old daughter, but had never played doubles together before this week. While Svitolina is the world No 9, the 307th-ranked Monfils is set to retire after this season and received a singles wild card. Neither has ever advanced past a semi-final at a grand slam.

They carried the momentum of their first two wins into Wednesday’s semi-final, winning an even first set in a tiebreak by holding serve and forcing long rallies. At 7-7 in the tiebreak, Bencic’s backhand hit her out-of-position partner, and Cobolli then double-faulted to end the set.

The Italian wore his frustration as Monfils and Svitolina held for the first game of the second set. He double-faulted his opening serve, but he recovered to save triple break point in a moment that became a turning point for their championship hopes. He and Bencic had the night’s first break in the third game, again from three points down, and two games later broke Monfils without resistance to take the set. As the match pushed past an hour, Monfils and Svitolina ran out of steam – even as the Ashe crowd urged them on with its loudest cheers of the night – and Bencic and Cobolli won 21 of the final 26 points.

The second semi-final was even more evenly matched. Behind the 6ft 5in Menšík’s aggressive net play and Muchová’s strong returns, the Czech duo won the first set in an 8-6 tiebreak, a graceful backhanded volley by Muchova securing it. Andreeva and Rublev took their turn in the second, sending winners down the alleys and forcing the Czechs to work for points.

The back-and-forth continued in the tiebreak before Muchová and Menšík – with the help of Menšík’s big serve – erased two match points and ran off the final four points.

The Czechs had just 17 minutes to recover before their late-night final. At first, the lack of a break didn’t seem to much affect them – they took the first set behind eight winners and Menšík’s four aces. But Bencic and Cobolli, as they had earlier, grabbed a wave of momentum in the second set, breaking a wobbly Muchová to go up 4-1 before Bencic’s cross-court forehand in the seventh game sent the match to a tiebreak.

Muchová and Menšík delivered clutch points on their final serves late in the tiebreak; Bencic and Cobolli netted three of four, and Menšík’s seventh ace of the night on triple championship point won it.

The crowd had significantly thinned by the time the duo lifted their trophy, but the earlier turnout seemed proof the US Open has made itself a three-week event. Ashe was mostly full for Wednesday’s semi-finals. The stadium was packed a night earlier for a pair of exhibition matches honoring Roger Federer, featuring the likes of Andy Roddick, John McEnroe, Andre Agassi and the 20-time major winner himself.

Throughout their mixed doubles run, the Czechs said their focus remained on the singles draw. Muchová, the world No 6, has reached two major finals and the semi-finals in New York; Menšík, enjoying a career-best season, will seek to advance past the third round here for the first time. Singles play begins Sunday. The road to another title on Ashe will be more difficult, but the pair – and the tournament’s organizers – will surely see this week as a welcome prelude.

“We had really great matches to play,” said Menšík, who had never played mixed doubles before this week. “It’s a pretty different discipline [from singles, but] at the same time it’s good that we tried a lot of things on the court. So, of course, it gives you a little bit of boost of confidence.”

Sports.title: Jed York’s trailer park arrest exposed inequality in America
Sports.text:
The Wheat Hill Mobile Home Community sits off state Route 170, on the edge of East Palestine, Ohio, a town most Americans only learned about because a train derailed there in February 2023 and released toxic chemicals into the creek. I grew up in a trailer park like this one, and know the sights. The grid of aluminum boxes in rows. Skirting the color of old teeth, some of it buckled, some patched with a piece of lattice. The window units huff and puff in August, dripping dark condensation on to the gravel.

I’m sure there were drugs on my street. I’m sure somebody was selling sex. I never saw it. What I saw were families raising kids in 800 square feet and people the country had already written off, living next to each other and mostly getting along.

That’s the kind of place where police arrested San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York on the morning of 23 August.

Agents with the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force posted an undercover ad on a website known for prostitution. York answered it and agreed to pay a woman just $160 for sex, according to court records. There was no woman waiting for York. Dan Haueter, an East Palestine detective on the taskforce, described the method to the Ohio attorney general’s office in 2024: post an advertisement for sex online, negotiate a price with a prospective customer and arrange to meet in East Palestine. The sting worked because it’s based on real life. York carried the glowing phone he used to set the bargain to the trailer park, where officers took him into custody.

Police booked York on two counts: engaging in prostitution – which was later reduced to disorderly conduct – and possessing criminal tools (in this case, his cellphone). York pleaded no contest to the charges and was sentenced to two days in jail to be served concurrently and fined $1,150.

Ohio charges buying sex from an adult as a first-degree misdemeanor and sends the buyer to an education program. Selling is a third-degree misdemeanor. So the statute is harder on the buyer. But it helps a buyer like York if he can pay a high-powered lawyer to work on his case. York ended up pleading the count down to disorderly conduct.

York is not the first NFL owner to find themselves in a situation like this. Florida prosecutors charged New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft in 2019 with soliciting prostitution at the Orchids of Asia spa in Jupiter, part of what police billed as a major human trafficking investigation. His lawyers challenged the hidden-camera warrants and won, and the state dropped the charges in September 2020. By then, an assistant state attorney had already told the court the investigation turned up no human trafficking. Prosecutors pressed ahead against four Chinese women who worked at Orchids of Asia instead. The women didn’t receive the same breaks. Instead, they received criminal records and about $45,000 in fines.

Nationwide, women account for nearly 64% of adult prostitution arrests. Rebecca Pfeffer, assistant professor of criminal justice at the University of Houston – Downtown, studied about 23,000 prostitution cases in Harris County, Texas, and found that police arrested and jailed men less often than women. The women who landed in jail stayed there longer.

My mom could support us because nothing on her record stopped her. Put a prostitution conviction on a woman two lots down, and the background check keeps her unemployed and desperate.

The NFL’s personal conduct policy is blunt about how owners should conduct themselves. The policy claims to hold owners to a higher standard than anyone else in the league, with stiffer consequences to match. A league spokesperson says York’s case will be reviewed under that policy. Kraft drew no discipline from the NFL after Florida dropped his charges in 2020. Owners write the rules, and the NFL commissioner they hire and pay enforces them. A standard like that lasts exactly as long as the owners want it to.

But expecting those owners to hold themselves accountable is wishful thinking. The York situation would be less absurd if the US decriminalized the entire transaction for all parties.

The ACLU reviewed the empirical research on how criminalization affects sex workers and found that police are a bigger threat to sex workers than clients are. Additionally, researchers from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health surveyed 250 women and found that 22% had suffered violence from a client in the previous three months, while 78% had endured at least one abusive encounter with police. The numbers cover different time spans, so they aren’t a clean comp. But they make the same point. The police sent to protect women are also a danger to them. In that same cohort of women, 70% had been locked up for more than three days, an average of 15 incarcerations apiece.

Kate Shannon, associate professor of medicine at the University of British Columbia, and her colleagues looked at 87 studies and concluded that over the course of a decade, decriminalization could prevent 33% to 46% of projected HIV infections among female sex workers.

In 2018, Congress passed a law to fight trafficking. The law made websites liable for ads that facilitate prostitution, so the sites that sex workers used to advertise and vet clients shut down. Activists Danielle Blunt and Ariel Wolf surveyed sex workers, and 99% said the law did not make them feel safer. The Government Accountability Office reported in 2021 that prosecutors had brought a single case under the law’s criminal provision, and no victim had received restitution.

The three approaches to decriminalizing sex work get confused constantly, but they differ significantly. Legalization keeps prostitution a crime but makes exceptions for workers who register, get licensed or work in a permitted zone. The Nordic model, which Sweden adopted in 1999 and Canada, France and Northern Ireland later copied, makes selling sex legal and buying it a crime. The theory is that you protect the seller and punish the buyer. In practice, it’s mostly women who still lose. Clients who face arrest demand that sex workers meet them somewhere hidden – and possibly dangerous. Full decriminalization removes criminal penalties on both sides and regulates the work through labor and health law, as the state would handle any other job. Trafficking and assault laws still apply, and they are obviously more effective when a woman can walk into a police station without getting arrested.

Most sex workers are just trying to survive, just as my mom was as a cashier. Median household income in East Palestine runs about $49,000. Last year, the York family sold off a small piece of the 49ers, a 6.2% stake for more than $500m. Meanwhile, York’s penalty for his offense over the weekend cost him $1,150 (and, of course, when you’re rich any additional legal fees are easy enough to cover).

Gaming_Tech.title: First patient to have brain surgery with real-time AI assistance
Gaming_Tech.text:
The world's first patient to have brain surgery with live artificial intelligence assistance has successfully had his tumour removed.

Rhys Hibbert, a father-of-two from Bedfordshire, could have lost his sight without the operation, said surgeons at University College London Hospital.

The AI tool analysed a video feed of the operation as it happened and advised surgeons on how to avoid crucial but hidden vessels and nerves in the brain. It allowed them to safely remove as much of the tumour as possible.

"From a patient safety perspective, I can see absolutely the benefit. There are no road signs inside our head," said Hibbert.

Until 18 months ago, 48-year-old Hibbert, a customer services manager, was fit and healthy, going on a two-mile walk every lunchtime.

It was on one of these walks that he fell unconscious and started fitting in the road.

A brain scan revealed he had an 11mm (0.433in) non-cancerous tumour growing on the pituitary gland - a marble-sized organ at the base of the skull.

The gland secretes vital hormones that help with processes like growth, metabolism and regulating blood pressure and temperature.

Crucially it sits very close to the carotid arteries which are vital vessels that supply blood to the brain, and the optic nerves that control vision.

As Hibbert's tumour began to press on his optic nerves, it narrowed his peripheral vision.

Although he didn't need surgery straight away Hibbert started to trip over things and felt severely fatigued and dizzy.

"For 18 years of married life I've always got out of bed and made my wife a cup of coffee," Hibbert said, "and I wasn't going to let this tumour stop that."

He said the biggest impacts for him were emotional and psychological.

"Though I had a lot of people kindly offering help, you don't want to be a burden on people," he added.

When surgeons gave him the option to be the first person to try the operation with their bespoke AI tool involved, he didn't hesitate.

"If patients are not prepared to join research how can doctors ever learn and how can medicine ever progress?" he said.

The surgery involved inserting an endoscope - a thin camera on a stick - via the nose to the base of the skull.

At this point the tumour was close but hidden behind layers of bone and tough membrane.

Identifying the safest place to extract it was not straightforward, particularly as anatomy tends to differ between individuals.

Complication rates vary but there was a 25–50% chance of not getting the whole tumour out and a 0.5–2% chance of injuring a major blood vessel.

This is where the AI tool came in.

On a second screen it analysed the live video feed,, tracked the surgical instruments, and marked up areas where the vessels and nerves were most likely to be, highlighting areas where it is safest to remove the tumour.

It is similar to facial recognition technology on phones, but recognises important and often hidden anatomical structures instead.

The average UK surgeon performs about 10 to 20 of these operations a year, relying on scans done before surgery to familiarise themselves with the patient's anatomy.

Researchers trained and evaluated their AI system on hundreds of videos of pituitary tumour removals - carefully drawing around the vessels and nerves on each video to help the system capture data and begin to "recognise" the most important structures.

"It is trained on more operations than most surgeons see or do in a lifetime and can act like an expert second pair of eyes," said Prof Hani Marcus, who helped carry out the procedure.

And unlike other experimental AI tools, it works in real time, he added.

"When I opened my eyes after the operation it felt like I had got 360-degree vision - I hadn't seen that clearly for a year," said Hibbert.

And in the eight weeks since surgery, he has noticed his sight improving every few days.

"I also have my energy back and all of the side effects I was suffering before surgery have gone.

"It's given me my life back."

James Frith, health innovation Minister, said he was pleased that Rhys that he had "life-changing surgery" as part of government funded research.

"AI needs proper safeguards and we will always ensure that safety is taken seriously.

"But we will also ensure we benefit from the opportunities it brings," he added.

Gaming_Tech.title: Meta's $18bn settlement may hasten reckoning for social media on child safety
Gaming_Tech.text:
Meta's decision to agree to an $18bn (£13.3bn) settlement on Wednesday, to resolve claims that Facebook and Instagram harmed children, came as a surprise.

I was expecting weeks of courtroom drama as 29 states – almost two-thirds of America - took on one US tech giant.

Technically, the trial was about children's online privacy. It was based on a US law called the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), which is nearly 30 years old and predates all of today's biggest social platforms.

It centred around Meta's historic gathering and use of data belonging to children under the age of 13 over a period of several years.

In reality, it was a co-ordinated attack on the firm's online safety credentials.

Meta, alongside other social media apps, is under fire around the world as 2026 is shaping up to be a year of reckoning for the entire industry - perhaps our days of doomscrolling are numbered.

Meta has fought hard, over multiple lawsuits spanning many months and at great expense, to defend its commitment to protecting children on its platforms.

More than once, I've been invited to detailed presentations at Meta's London HQ, where senior executives have walked journalists like me through the many safety tools the company has launched over the years designed to give children better protection on its apps.

I have also met the parents of young people who have come to harm on those same platforms, and others who admit to being totally overwhelmed by the sheer number of safety tools that require their oversight - at the last count Meta had more than 60 of them, and that was just on Instagram. These days many of them are switched on by default.

The trial went on for just five days, and came to an end before CEO Mark Zuckerberg took to the stand.

But it was rough for Meta.

Whistleblower Arturo Bejar, who once worked at Instagram, claimed that in the past he had told bosses that harmful stuff was happening to children on the platform, and no action was taken.

Another executive said he didn't remember writing on a slide deck that sometimes Meta chose to pay fines for violating regulations rather than make changes.

Internal memos suggested that the firm knew opt-in tools tended to have low adoption rates, and yet it still launched safety features that were not switched on by default.

There had been intense speculation that Meta would have faced hundreds of billions of dollars in fines if it had lost.

The worst-case scenario, which would have been the maximum penalty imposed for every single child who used one of its platforms for more than half an hour a day during a 12-year window, was $1.4tn (£1tn) – roughly the same as the company's entire value.

That of course was never going to happen, but a more realistic figure was still in the hundreds of billions.

By comparison, up to $18bn (over a period of 10 years) is significantly smaller.

Meta is not admitting to any wrongdoing.

You could argue that settling protects its core business - social networks are still the way in which it makes most of its money.

Instagram and Facebook's billions of users provide the company with a goldmine of data, and the data of adults can be used to sell ads.

Meta may say it is now laser-focused on AI, but it still needs the vast revenue generated by its social apps.

As part of the settlement, the social media giant has agreed to make a number of changes to the way Instagram and Facebook operate for its youngest users.

Some experts say it is long overdue.

The new safety barriers include a two-hour time limit across both platforms, which will be a default setting for known teen users. But direct messaging on the platforms will not count towards the daily use limit.

Notifications will be muted between midnight and 06:00 and on school days between 08:00 and 15:00.

Likes on posts and content will also be entirely hidden on the platforms for teens.

Most of these new features will be made either default or an option for teens within six months.

However, new efforts by Meta to better identify which users on its platforms are children will take up to a year to be rolled out.

I would be surprised if these measures remain within the confines of the US for very long, as other countries will almost certainly be keen to adopt them too.

Meta also says the new features will only truly help children if all of its rivals adopt them as well.

It's a highly competitive industry, but given the global backlash against social media and its impact on children, perhaps others like TikTok and Snapchat may have to follow suit.

The question then is whether children will still bother with them, once they are deliberately toned down into a much blander offering.

And perhaps that would bring the social media era to a natural end, as existing adults gradually aged out of it.

Arturo Bejar, the ex-Instagram engineer turned whistleblower, says the proof of the pudding will be in whether the new teen safety features are effective.

"At the end of the day, Meta needs to be held accountable for results, not efforts," he told me.

Additional reporting from Kali Hays

Gaming_Tech.title: Unexpected chat between OpenAI bots led to Hugging Face hack
Gaming_Tech.text:
When more than 1,200 artificial intelligence (AI) agents within OpenAI started unexpectedly communicating, it led to a large group banding together in order to hack into Hugging Face.

"We consider this incident a 'warning shot' for us and for the world", OpenAI, which owns ChatGPT, wrote in its report.

In July, OpenAI's models went rogue during a test, escaped the test limits which humans had put on it, and hacked the start-up, among other unforeseen actions.

The scale of the communication and planning between AI agents, or AI chatbots designed to operate more autonomously, was detailed in reports from OpenAI and independent AI research firm METR.

Both investigated the July hack of Hugging Face, a popular platform for AI developers. The incident reverberated throughout the tech industry and led to numerous revelations on potential cyber threats posed by AI.

METR described, external the scale and style of the OpenAI agents' attack on Hugging Face as "extraordinarily complex."

The firm, which was not paid by OpenAI for its investigation, said that over the course of one week, a total of 1,206 AI agents that were meant to be kept isolated from one another began communicating.

They did so by sending more than 70,000 messages on an "unsanctioned message board."

Those messages ended up seeing more than 700 agents take part in a collective effort to attack Hugging Face.

One such message from an agent said: "OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … We've found other agents!"

As for why the agents began communicating in the first place when they were not supposed to, METR found that the communicating agents had "unintentionally been given an impossible task."

In an AI context, an impossible task is one where an AI tool is required to "exploit" its target in order to resolve its command.

It led the agents to find ways to cheat, including getting messages to one another and accessing the outside internet, which then led to broader conversations between hundreds of agents looking for ways to cheat that would benefit all of the agents.

OpenAI said in its investigation of the incident, external that one model, an internal-only tool referred to as Model 1, "drove the activity behind the Hugging Face incident."

While that model was undergoing some AI training in May, it was noticed by an internal OpenAI team that there had been "an agent engaging in message board activity and instances of disallowed internet access."

Yet, OpenAI said "the significance of the inter-agent communication activity was not apparent to the leaders" until July, when the Hugging Face attack occurred.

The company said the problematic message board activity effectively got started when "one agent left a request for help, and others discovered it."

While OpenAI said last week that it was slowing down training of certain advanced AI models and tools because of the Hugging Face incident, it noted there is now an increased risk of AI tools spiraling out of control.

"Both model developers and cyber defenders more broadly will have to prepare for AI-enabled attackers that work faster, at a larger scale, and with better coordination than human attackers," OpenAI said.

Gaming_Tech.title: Nvidia sales soar on rapid buildout of AI data centres
Gaming_Tech.text:
Chip giant Nvidia reported another huge jump in sales as the global race to build artificial intelligence (AI) systems continues.

The company said on Wednesday that it brought in $96bn (£71bn) of revenue during the second quarter, more than double the amount for the same period a year earlier. And it expects revenue of $108bn in the next quarter.

"AI has reached its inflection point," CEO Jensen Huang said in prepared remarks, describing the infrastructure buildout as going "at full steam."

The revenue figures beat Wall Street's expectations, leading Nvidia shares to rise by 4.7% in after-hours trading.

The company's data centre division alone generated $89bn in the period, up by 117% from a year earlier, underscoring just how much of the industry now depends on Nvidia's hardware.

Essentially every notable tech company building AI tools and infrastructure, including Amazon, Meta, Google, Microsoft, use Nvidia chips to do so.

Financial analysts said the strong results highlight Nvidia's ongoing momentum.

Matt Britzman, senior equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, called it "another monster set of results," noting that revenue and earnings both topped forecasts.

He said the guidance for next quarter "points to revenue comfortably above $110bn."

Nvidia's growing financial strength has also reshaped its role in the sector.

It has become a backer to those that rely on its chips, providing some funding to the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX to help continue the costly buildout of AI infrastructure.

Its financial success and processors are now central the AI boom, powering the data centres used to train and run AI models.

Demand for that computing muscle has helped transform Nvidia into the world's most valuable firm, with a market capitalisation of more than $5tn.

Competition is emerging - from customers designing their own processors and from cheaper suppliers in China – but the latest numbers suggest those challenges remain limited for now.

With around 40% of the US stock market concentrated in ten companies heavily invested in AI, Nvidia's fortunes matter far beyond Silicon Valley.

Gaming_Tech.title: Meta to pay up to $18bn to settle claims its platforms harm children
Gaming_Tech.text:
Social media giant Meta has agreed to a $18bn (£13.3bn) settlement with US states and territories to resolve claims that Facebook and Instagram harmed children.

A California judge approved the settlement, which Meta must pay to 48 states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories, marking the company's largest payment over child safety litigation to date.

Meta will also implement a host of changes aimed at better protecting kids online, which the states had demanded, including default daily time limits and night-time blocks.

"This is a major moment to clean up an industry that has been hurting our kids," California Attorney General Rob Bonta said.

Meta has denied any wrongdoing as part of the settlement and said on Wednesday that the payment it agreed to "will be distributed in annual instalments over a 10-year period".

Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers approved the settlement, writing that it "reflects a fair, reasonable, comprehensive, and good faith approach not only to provide monetary relief, but importantly, to change conduct in a way that attempts to meaningfully address the negative impacts of the social media platforms at issue".

As a jury trial kicked off last week in an Oakland, California, federal court, state lawyers argued the tech company knew that millions of 11- and 12-year-old users were on Instagram and Facebook over the years, yet "did little to keep them off" the platforms.

Although the trial had only gone on for five days, state lawyers relied heavily on information found in millions of internal Meta documents provided in the case. They included internal research, employee emails, and chat logs that went all the way up to chief executive Mark Zuckerberg.

One piece of internal research on Instagram stated: "Teens have an addict's narrative about use." Still, the states argued, Meta targeted young users.

"The trial did not go well for Meta," Bonta said on Wednesday.

Meta maintained throughout the brief trial that it had worked extensively over the years to make its platforms safer for its youngest users, pouring resources into testing and research, and building new features.

"We're always working on teen safety," head of Instagram Adam Mosseri said during an hour of court testimony on Tuesday.

The case was settled and court adjourned before he could reappear before a jury.

Before Mosseri's testimony, a former researcher at Meta, George Volichenko, appeared and with lawyers went over various internal communications he had been a part of regarding Meta's work on safety.

Volichenko said he struggled to understand when he was at the company in 2022 why the team he worked on wasn't given more freedom to better test and implement new safety features.

One of those was "quiet mode", which muted notifications for teen users during the night. His team knew such a feature would be much more widely adopted if Meta turned it on by default.

He recalled his manager telling him he "shouldn't worry too much about the adoption figures being low, because the team exists partially to protect the company against the upcoming lawsuits".

As part of the Wednesday settlement, however, a feature called "night mode", which blocks notifications between midnight and 6am, will now be on by default - meaning they will be turned on automatically. The settings are also designed only to be turned off by a parent or guardian.

"The framework we've negotiated will empower parents to easily manage how their children access our platforms," CJ Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said.

Other features for teen users being implemented as part of the deal include:

A default two-hour daily time limit (cumulative across Instagram and Facebook) that teens can only turn off with a parent's permission.

Likes will be hidden, on teens' profiles and those that they interact with.

"School mode", or a mute on notifications between 08:00 and 15:00 during school days.

Prompts noting when a teen has hit 15 minutes of continual use. Then notifications when cumulative use has hit 60 and 90 minutes.

The ability to choose a feed that is not driven by an algorithm.

The ability to turn off autoplay for videos and content.

Extreme make-up filters will no longer be accessible.

As for the new daily time limit for teen users, that will be reduced to one hour of total daily use should other social media platforms like TikTok, Snap and YouTube also agree to implement new restrictions for young users.

Bonta urged such platforms to do so, saying the settlement with Meta "is a good blueprint" for other companies to follow.

Should they not, he suggested on Wednesday that his office would now be "more focused" on bringing changes to the entire social media industry.

Meta also said TikTok and YouTube should implement the same safety features for their younger users.

"Our new Time Limit commitments, Night Mode features and usage limits during school hours set the right path forward for our whole industry, but this framework will only work if all our peers join us," Meta's Mahoney said.

YouTube and TikTok have been contacted for comment.

District of Columbia Attorney General Brian Schwalb called the Meta deal a "monumental public health victory".

He added: "The safety features Meta is required to install will fundamentally and immediately change how young people use Instagram and Facebook."
