Entertainment.title: Yayoi Kusama, Japanese artist who became a global superstar, dies aged 97
Entertainment.text:
Yayoi Kusama, the Japanese outsider artist who reached superstar status after decades living in a psychiatric hospital, has died aged 97.

Kusama died in a Tokyo hospital on 14 August, her company Yayoi Kusama Inc announced in a statement on Thursday.

“Throughout an extraordinary lifetime devoted entirely to artistic creation, Kusama pursued an internationally acclaimed career as a pioneering avant garde artist whose creative practice encompassed visual art, performance, fiction, and poetry,” the statement read. “She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush, and continued exploration of forever love and eternal soul.”

“We will carry forward Kusama’s wishes and, through art, continue to bring hope and strength for the future to people around the world.”

Instantly recognisable by her bright red bobbed wig, Kusama became known for her psychedelic colour schemes and “infinity mirror room” installations, which helped her find a huge audience in the age of the social media selfie: her 2024 show in Australia was the most popular exhibition in the country’s history. Yet she had pioneered many of her enduring themes as a young artist in the 1960s, before fading into temporary obscurity.

As well as being a sculptor and painter, Kusama put on numerous performance pieces throughout the hippy era that saw her name attached to scandal. She staged “body festivals” with naked performers painted in polka dots and once wrote to US president Richard Nixon offering to sleep with him in return for an end to the Vietnam war. News of such events appalled her conservative family back home.

Kusama was born in Matsumoto, Japan, in 1929, enduring an unhappy childhood at the hands of an abusive mother and philandering father. Her wealthy family managed plant nurseries and Kusama would sit and draw the flowers despite her mother’s frequent attempts to stop her. As a child, Kusama began experiencing hallucinations, in which the flowers would swarm around and talk to her. Her coping mechanism was to draw what she saw.

During the second world war, 13-year-old Kusama was conscripted to produce fabric for Japanese army parachutes. She later studied nihonga, a traditional Japanese style of painting, in Kyoto, but grew frustrated with its limitations. Rejecting her planned future of an arranged marriage and children, Kusama left Japan for New York in 1958. There, she fell in with the artist and theorist Donald Judd and made a breakthrough with her “infinity net” paintings – vast fields of impastoed polka dots that stretched across the canvas. In 1962, she sold her first of these to the artists Frank Stella and Judd for $75. In 2014, her White No 28 sold for $7.1m (£5.7m) at auction, a record at the time for a living female artist.

In 1963, Kusama started making “soft sculptures” – pieces of furniture and other objects, such as ladders, covered with white, fabric-stuffed phallic shapes. They were, she said, her attempt to heal her disgust around sex, which she had been brought up to believe was dirty and shameful.

Despite working loosely within the spheres of pop art and minimalism, Kusama was not embraced by the art world. She always maintained that many of her ideas from this period were appropriated by white male artists, including Andy Warhol, while she was written out of art history.

Kusama’s work was often centred around the infinite and the idea of “self-obliteration”, a concept inspired by the hallucinations that would engulf her. Talking about her 1954 painting Flower (DSPS), she once said: “I was looking at the red flower patterns of the tablecloth on a table, and when I looked up I saw the same pattern covering the ceiling, the windows and the walls, and finally all over the room, my body and the universe. I felt as if I had begun to self-obliterate, to revolve in the infinity of endless time and the absoluteness of space, and be reduced to nothingness.”

At the 1966 Venice Biennale she continued these studies, presenting her infamous Narcissus Garden, a “lake” of 1,500 reflective balls that strived for a sense of mirrored infinity. When Kusama began selling the balls for $2 each under the banner “Your narcissism for sale”, the biennale moved to close the operation down.

Kusama developed a flair for controversy. Her artistic “happenings” were often criticised for being mere shock material, yet their political statements now seem ahead of their time. In 1968, she staged New York’s first “homosexual wedding” in Tribeca and washed a “dirty” Soviet flag outside the United Nations building in protest over the invasion of Czechoslovakia.

By this time Kusama was engaged in a platonic yet obsessive relationship with the outsider artist Joseph Cornell, which continued even after she had left the US to return to Japan. She had been frequently admitted to hospital during her time in New York and when Cornell died in 1972, her mental health deteriorated further, with hallucinations, panic attacks and suicide attempts. In 1977, she checked herself into a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo that offered art therapy courses and provided Kusama with the stability needed to pursue her projects without distraction. She made the decision to live there permanently, working each day from morning until night in her nearby studio.

Although she published several novels during the 1980s, interest in Kusama appeared to have waned almost completely by the start of the 90s. But the recognition that eluded her during her early artistic career finally arrived later in life. In 1993 she created a mirrored room filled with small pumpkin sculptures for the Venice Biennale’s Japanese pavilion and won plaudits for the work. She had first seen a pumpkin with her grandfather when she was 11. When she tried to pick it, it had appeared to start speaking to her, and now it became a recurring motif in works such as All the Eternal Love I Have for the Pumpkins, from 2016.

Kusama’s focus shifted towards installations that built on her 1965 work Infinity Mirror Room: Phalli’s Field. In that piece, hundreds of soft, pink phallic forms were arranged within a mirrored room. Half a century later, such immersive experiences connected with audiences on a global scale, with the coloured lights and brightly painted pumpkins providing perfect Instagram content. It was not without irony that an exhibition of hers at the Hirshhorn Museum in Washington DC in 2017 was temporarily closed after someone damaged an artwork while attempting to take a selfie.

Kusama received retrospectives at the New York’s Museum of Modern Art in 1998, Tate Modern in London in 2012 and Washington DC’s Hirshhorn Museum in 2017. Tickets for her shows sold out swiftly around the world and fans would queue for hours just to be allowed a 30-second experience within her installations.

Despite some critics wondering if she had become the world’s most popular artist, Kusama always believed that her place in history would not be decided by the art establishment.

Entertainment.title: Jeers, walkouts, stage invasions: will Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists trigger British audiences too?
Entertainment.text:
In February, turbulent scenes inside a German theatre made headlines around the globe. During the final act of a play at Schauspielhaus theatre in Bochum, the audience first jeered and whistled at a performer in the role of a far-right politician. An orange lobbed from the auditorium narrowly missed its target; eventually, two spectators climbed on to the stage and tried to wrestle the actor off. News of the incident travelled around the world: it seemed a bizarre throwback to a world in which people were not able to tell the difference between art and real life, like 19th-century Parisians stampeding out of a cinema after watching a train hurtle towards the camera.

For the man who wrote the play, however, it was nothing unusual. “I was not surprised by the reaction,” says Portuguese playwright Tiago Rodrigues. “I was surprised by the fact that it was so surprising for so many people.” He describes the audience’s reaction to his play Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists as “very intense”, but also “typical”.

The play, which visits London’s National Theatre next month, tells the story of a macabre family tradition: once every year, a group of relatives gather over a feast of wild boar and asparagus in the southern Portuguese countryside to kill a fascist they have kidnapped. Their ritual is designed to avenge the real-life murder of Catarina Eufémia, a harvester in revolt who was killed at the hands of the Salazar regime’s police force in 1954. But this year the family member tasked with the execution voices some doubts about the ritual’s righteousness, and things go awry: in the play’s last half hour, the freed fascist gives a victory speech that is uninterrupted by the rest of the cast. Ever since its September 2020 premiere in Guimarães, audiences have stepped in to intervene.

In Portugal, spectators chanted Grândola, Vila Morena, José Afonso’s song of the 1974 Carnation revolution, to drown out the actor’s words. In Italy, they sang anti-fascist resistance anthem Bella Ciao. In Austria, spectators stood up and walked out. There were attempts to storm the stage and hit the actor impersonating the fascist politician at performances in Lisbon, Paris, Marseille and in Montreal. In other places, it was the far right that expressed its indignation: the Rome premiere of Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists was met with protests from the local branch prime minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party, which asked for the play to be removed from the programme.

“We always get these reactions, whether we’re in Switzerland or in Norway,” Rodrigues says, matter-of-factly. “In around 200 performances, we’ve had perhaps a handful of shows where the audience just listened to the final speech in silence.”

What is it about his play that has made it a 21st-century equivalent of Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring, triggering mini-riots wherever it is shown? One answer may be that Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists is essentially two plays in one, each of which annuls the answers offered by the other: an anti-fascist play that asks difficult questions of both liberal and militant anti-fascists.

For the first two hours, Rodrigues’s play is a reflection on what the philosopher Karl Popper called the “paradox of tolerance”: to preserve an open and tolerant society, must we be intolerant towards those who advocate intolerance? Or does our society cease to be a tolerant one when we do so? The second question carries particular weight in Rodrigues’s staging, for the anti-fascist tradition that the family at the heart of the play represents is one that comes across as self-absorbed, self-regarding and, in its own way, reactionary. “Our family killed fascists during the dictatorship, we killed fascists during the democracy and will continue to kill fascists,” says one of the characters, Pedro. “You shouldn’t ask yourself ‘Why?’ or ‘Why also me?’. The real ‘why’ is in the ‘how’. There’s a method, a ritual, a tradition, a beauty.”

It’s hard not to side with Sara, the young woman who has been chosen to kill her first fascist this year but instead of duty feels only doubt. Is killing not like imposing a dictatorship, she asks: “Death, where you don’t think, don’t argue, where you can’t change your mind, is that not the greatest dictatorship of all?” And if the end supposedly justifies the means, why has their ritual not managed to fend off fascism for good (in the play, the extreme right has recently gained power over Portugal again)? “Why don’t we have a revolution, a coup d’état, a guerrilla campaign, a war? Why don’t we kill all the fascists once and for all and get this thing sorted?”

Rodrigues, who has been artistic director of the D’Avignon theatre festival since 2022, does not hide his sympathies with Sara’s inner conflict. “My own views are quite simple,” he says. “I consider the far right an enemy that has to be fought, but we should fight them in a democratic way, and if that doesn’t work, you keep on playing it democratic. I think most of the audience usually position themselves in a similar way: they feel Sara is right.

“Nevertheless, there have been moments in history where violence was considered a legitimate response to fascism. Where I live today, in the south of France, I don’t think it’s controversial to say that armed resistance was a legitimate answer to the Nazi occupation.”

With the family of anti-fascists unable to come to a collective decision on how to address their problem, the fascist politician is freed and gives a victory speech straight out of the modern far right’s rulebook, decrying the dictatorship of “minorities” over “the people”, the biased mainstream media, the intolerant liberal left. If you overthink your anti-fascism, Rodrigues seems to be saying in response to the first part of the play, this is what you get.

The playwright says he wrote the final monologue during the rehearsals. “We had this problem: how do we finish? If Sara’s side won, it would be very didactic and politically correct. And I realised the victory of the far right would be the most troubling, the most dystopian and also the most thought-provoking.” His own cast’s response to the ending foreshadowed the reactions the play has received around the globe. “Some people felt sick, others were in tears and left the room or thought about quitting the project altogether. There were a lot of debates about whether we have the right to put such a speech on stage today.”

He condemns those who have tried to assault members of his cast, but says it’s not for him to judge spectators shouting down a fascist speech: “It’s not something that we find to be a mistake.” Some viewers, he believes, feel the play is inviting them to react in a visceral way: “They feel they have to show emotion because the actor is addressing them, and if they don’t protest they are accomplices of his speech. For them, it’s a kind of game they’ve been invited to play.”

In other cases, he suggests, the outrage may also cloak a deeper feeling of helplessness: “The audience have spent two hours following a complex debate and worked out their own position within it, and suddenly that choice is not there any more. That’s very disturbing. Some of the same people who agreed most strongly with Sara that the left should not use violence are the loudest to scream ‘kill him’ at the end of the play.”

Rodrigues decided to tackle the question of how societies can protect themselves from fascism after André Ventura, the founder of anti-immigration party Chega, in 2019 became the first far-right politician to be elected as a member of Portugal’s parliament since the end of the Salazar regime. Until that point, the Iberian country had looked immune to the brand of rightwing populism that was rattling most countries in Europe.

“I remember when I mentioned in rehearsals that the story would be about a victory for the far right in 2028. Everybody laughed: yeah, that’s never going to happen, eight years is too short. And I agreed with it. My defence was that we needed to exaggerate to focus the audience’s mind.” Today, Chega is the second largest party in Portuguese politics; earlier this year, Ventura came second in a rare runoff vote for the presidency.

“As a playwright, you are sometimes dystopian because you don’t want to be prophetic,” he adds. “Unfortunately, reality keeps making this piece more relevant.”

BreakingNewsTab.title: Aunt who died in Middlesbrough house fire was 'beautiful soul'
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A woman killed in a house fire has been described by her mother as "a beautiful soul, who would have done anything for anybody".

Natalie McDonald, 34, died along with her seven-year-old niece, Valentina Foster, in the blaze in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of Wednesday.

Cleveland Police said the fire had also left a 48-year-old woman in a critical condition in hospital alongside another three people who suffered non-life threatening injuries.

Two men, aged 23 and 31, had been arrested on suspicion of murder and were in police custody, the force said.

Lisa Kirton, Natalie's mother, told the BBC her daughter was "lovely, bright and bubbly" and "everybody loved her".

She said Valentina, also known as Tina, had been spending the summer holidays with the family.

"She was a cute little kid," Kirton said. "I can't believe it, seven years old - it's just a disgrace."

She also said Natalie's 15-year-old daughter and a friend had managed to escape through an upstairs window.

The friend, she said, had "kicked out a window" and "had saved their lives".

A 20-year-old neighbour told the BBC how local residents had tried to rescue the occupants.

Ellie, who did not want to give her surname, said: "The entire house was scorching.

"I couldn't get near the front of the house, it was that hot."

She described holding the hand of a crying woman who had jumped from an upstairs window, staying with her until paramedics arrived.

A neighbour, who asked not to be named, said: "My daughter heard shouting and screaming this morning. The dogs were barking."

On Wednesday, Police officers guarded a cordon around the scene and Northern Powergrid staff were also on site.

Cleveland Fire Brigade said it had sent six fire engines and the Incident Command Unit.

At 13:30 BST it confirmed the fire had been extinguished, but one engine remained on "proactive standby".

A spokesperson said road closures were in place and asked members of the public to avoid the area where possible.

They also said the "tragic incident" was being jointly investigated by the fire service and Cleveland Police.

Cleveland Police said it was "keeping an open mind and cannot rule out any links to wider organised crime at this time".

The fire happened about two miles from the A66 crash that killed five young men and two police officers on Saturday morning.

Redcar and Cleveland Local Policing Commander Supt Emily Harrison said the force was working to "establish the circumstances of exactly what has happened".

"We will have a high visibility presence in the Grangetown area and encourage anyone who has concerns, or who may have information, to approach our officers."

Patrols had been increased in the local area to "reassure the local community", the force said earlier.

Grangetown councillor Adam Brook urged people not to speculate or share unconfirmed information.

Redcar MP Anna Turley said the community had faced a "profound amount of heartbreak over the past few weeks" and expressed her condolences to the loved ones of those who died and were injured.

The families of the people involved have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Yayoi Kusama: Japanese avant-garde artist dies aged 97
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Japanese avant-garde artist Yayoi Kusama, who became famous for her colourful polka dot-covered sculptures and installations, has died at the age of 97.

Kusama, who had voluntarily lived in a psychiatric hospital for decades, was known for her bright red wig and her giant, quirky creations.

Her exhibitions drew large crowds around the world, and her vibrant works fetched some of the highest ever prices for a female artist.

A statement from her company said: "Throughout an extraordinary lifetime devoted entirely to artistic creation, Kusama pursued an internationally acclaimed career as a pioneering avant-garde artist whose creative practice encompassed visual art, performance, fiction, and poetry."

Kusama died at a hospital in Tokyo on 14 August, the statement said.

It added: "She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush, and continued exploration of forever love and eternal soul.

"We will carry forward Kusama's wishes and, through art, continue to bring hope and strength for the future to people around the world."

Kusama became one of the world's most recognisable artists and a global cultural icon in her 80s and 90s, after having been mostly overlooked for decades.

Poorly received by a masculine-dominated art scene of New York in the 1960s, Kusama caused a stir with her exhibitions of phallic sculptures, including a fabric couch, and frequent displays of nudity.

In 1965, her work "Infinity Mirror Rooms", in which mirrors and lights create seemingly endless spaces, attracted millions of visitors. Later, her polka dot and pumpkin works became highly sought-after.

However, she became distressed when her ideas were copied by or "inspired" her male contemporaries – including Andy Warhol, Claes Oldenburg and Lucas Samaras – whose works would be displayed at more prestigious galleries.

After spending years watching male artists gain recognition for her work, she returned home to Japan – feeling dejected and distraught.

She entered a psychiatric facility receiving treatment for mental illnesses, where she would live and work for the remainder of her life.

Miraculously, she managed to find a hospital where the doctors were interested in art therapy and checked herself in. Such a secure environment allowed her to focus on creating art.

Through the 1970s and early 80s, her work depicted uncharacteristically dark series' of collages in which she embraced the imagery of natural life cycles.

Kusama went on to become Japan's first solo artist to represent the country at the 1993 Venice Biennale. Twenty-seven years earlier, she had turned up, uninvited, and laid down 1,500 mirror balls on the ground.

The roaring success of the exhibition led to a huge transformation in how she was received both in Japan and abroad.

In 2001, she was awarded the Asahi Prize – recognising outstanding cultural, academic and artistic contributions in Japan.

One of her paintings fetched about $10.5m (£7.7m) at auction in 2022, making her works some of the highest-earning in the world for a female artist.

Then, her work appeared in major museums and collaborations with luxury brands including Louis Vuitton.

The world, along with her native Japan, radically changed its perception of Kusama in her later life.

Social media fuelled a spike in interest over recent years – with her museum's bold floral shapes and shiny steel orbs turning into a desired backdrop for selfies and poses.

Among her many motifs, the pumpkin has become iconic in her works. To her, the vegetable represented comfort and nostalgia.

She once said in an interview, "Pumpkins speak to me."

"They embody a sense of stability and gives me peace of mind."

In her hometown of Naoshima, visitors coming by ferry are greeted by her outdoor Red Pumpkin sculpture covered in bold, black polka dots.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Two dead and 11 hurt after car rams into crowd in northern France
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Two people have been killed and 10 others injured after a car crashed into a group of people near a train station in Caen in northern France, French reports say.

"A car deliberated rammed into pedestrians opposite the station," local prefect David Clavière told reporters, adding that seven of those injured were in a critical condition.

A man was later arrested after authorities launched a major emergency response in the wider Normandy region.

Caen Mayor Aristide Olivier said investigators were trying to understand what had led to the driver's actions. Witnesses said a fight had broken out between two groups before the incident took place.

"For the moment, we are not dealing with a terrorist motive, but the investigation is only just beginning," said Bruno Coutanceau, a top security official for Caen.

All of the victims appeared to be men between the ages of 17 and 40, he told AFP.

The suspect, a 26-year-old man born in Russia, was later arrested around 20km (12 miles) away in the port town of Ouistreham.

The mayor of Caen later told local media his car had been tracked by the city's CCTV network.

He was not previously known to intelligence services and police had been aware of him "only for traffic offences", Clavière said.

Social media videos from the scene appeared to show crowds gathering around police cars and ambulances, where a large area was cordoned off.

A spokesperson for the local administration of Calvados told the BBC that some of those injured were receiving treatment in the emergency ward of a nearby hospital.

Police have opened an investigation into the incident, which will be led by detectives from Caen's Specialised Crime Division.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Burnham calls summit of first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The prime minister says he will bring together the first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland in the autumn for a summit.

Andy Burnham made the announcement ahead of a visit to south Wales on Thursday - his first official visit to the country since he took control of the UK government.

The Labour leader said he wanted "every leader in this country signed up" to having "good jobs in every community".

Downing Street said the first ministers of Wales and Scotland, and the first and deputy first ministers of Northern Ireland will meet the prime minister at the National Economic Council in October.

Former Greater Manchester mayor Burnham took over from Sir Keir Starmer in July, after winning the Makerfield by-election.

Burnham is visiting a location in south Wales as part of his listening tour.

His spokespeople said he will speak to Welsh workers and apprentices about "reindustrialisation, jobs and the cost of living".

Burnham said: "I am in South Wales today because the answers to the UK's challenges will not come from an echo chamber. They will come from the places that know their own strengths, and from a government willing to listen and then act.

"Good jobs in every community, in every part of the UK. That is what I want every leader in this country signed up to."

He will meet the Welsh government's deputy first minister Sioned Williams at the visit.

Williams said the visit was "a positive example of governments working together to improve people's lives".

She will call for a "fair share of the UK government's steel fund", an "energy social tariff to support those facing fuel poverty and struggling with high energy bills", and high standing charges in Wales to be addressed.

She added: "Wales is an energy-rich nation. People should see that reflected in good jobs, stronger communities and lower bills."

The National Economic Council was created by the Gordon Brown administration in 2008, and has been revived by Burnham.

A previous meeting brought together government ministers and English local authority mayors.

Downing Street said the prime minister wanted to discuss "how we will drive good growth in every postcode across the UK" with the first ministers.

The Welsh government said: "We look forward to discussing shared challenges, including ensuring growth and investment in all the countries represented, and support for families facing the continuing cost-of-living crisis.

"This is alongside further discussions with the UK government to progress broader priorities in Wales, including fair funding and extending devolution."

Plaid Cymru has pressed the UK government for discussions over more powers and funding for the Senedd - Wales's parliament - and the Welsh government in Cardiff.

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth had his first meeting with the new prime minister on the sidelines of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games in July.

At the time, ap Iorwerth said it was "too early" to know whether the new Labour prime minister would agree to his calls.

Downing Street said then that the prime minister wanted an "open and ongoing dialogue" with the first minister.

Welsh Liberal Democrat MP David Chadwick said Wales "needs action" if the prime minister is serious about "easing the burden on Welsh families".

BreakingNewsTab.title: UK weather: Thunderstorm warnings continue with more rain expected
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Met Office yellow warnings will remain in force for most of Thursday as heavy rain and thunderstorms move northwards across the UK.

An initial warning that covered south-east England for the early morning has now expired, but another one covers a broader swathe of England and Wales and is valid until 22:00 BST.

Downpours will continue to bring the risk of flash flooding and travel disruption.

The wettest areas could potentially see 75mm (3in) of rain, accompanied by large hail, lightning and gusty winds.

It will also feel rather humid for many.

Spells of rain are set to continue over the weekend - a bank holiday for England, Wales and Northern Ireland - accompanied by windy conditions in the south.

It was a wet start to Thursday in southern England and south Wales, with Herstmonceux in East Sussex recording 21.4mm (0.8in) of rain in six hours overnight, according to the Met Office.

Widespread thunderstorms have also been spreading across Wales, the Midlands and parts of eastern England with tricky driving conditions for morning commuters.

Those showers and storms will arrive in northern England by the early afternoon.

As this initial zone of downpours clears northwards the skies will brighten and sunny spells will develop, but further scattered showers are possible.

These could, again, be very heavy and thundery.

Some rain is likely to arrive in parts of Northern Ireland and Scotland late in the day, although these northern areas of the UK are likely to avoid the very wettest weather.

Within the Met Office yellow warning area, 20-30mm (0.8-1.2in) of rain could fall in just a few hours, with up to 50mm (2in) over a 12-hour period.

Hills exposed to the easterly wind could possibly see 75mm (3in).

Hazardous driving conditions are expected with a chance that roads will be closed and communities cut off.

Lightning strikes could lead to power cuts, and hailstones of 1-2cm (0.4-0.8in) are also possible.

The wet weather will be welcome news for the large areas of England and Wales that remain in drought, however there is the increased risk of flash flooding where the ground is very dry and hard.

Not enough rain will fall to alleviate the recent dry spell, with experts warning that months of persistent wet weather is needed to replenish water supplies.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Plug-in solar panels are coming to a shop near you - what to know
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Plug-in solar panels will be hitting the shelves of DIY shops and High Street retailers after the government changed the rules to allow them to be legally sold in the UK.

They are significantly cheaper than roof panels, can be installed without an electrician and are suitable for properties with outdoor space, including some balconies.

Retailers including Argos will be stocking products from Thursday, and the government expects other shops to follow suit.

It hopes plug-in solar panels will help households save money and reduce reliance on overseas fuel sources, the price of which has fluctuated in recent months due to the Middle East conflict.

Customers should get their wiring checked by a professional to ensure it is safe before parting with cash, experts say.

The government hopes the plug-in panels will offer people a more affordable way into solar energy compared to roof installation, although savings will be lower because they generate less power.

A one-panel kit will cost £699 while two-panels will be £1,089, according to UK solar company UKSOL.

The current regulations only allow people to plug in one device per property, but this may be changed in future.

The government expects prices to settle at £400-£600 as competition increases and more products are developed.

Its research shows a household could save between £70 and £110 a year on their energy bills.

The precise amount will depend on how the panels are orientated and how long they run. An unshaded south-facing spot is best.

Households which use energy during daylight hours will benefit most as the electricity must be used as it is generated.

Any power not consumed will flow back to the grid, but it's unlikely homes will get any cash for this.

Unlike rooftop solar panels, these systems do not need to be certified under the official Microgeneration Certification Scheme (MCS), which is the UK's official quality mark for small-scale renewable energy systems.

But it also means they will not normally qualify for the Smart Export Guarantee that pays people for excess solar power.

The panels will make a difference to a household's power consumption but it is deliberately modest for safety reasons.

While kits may come with panels that are capable of generating more power, the microinverter - which turns the current from the panel into electricity homes can use - will limit output to the home to 800 watts.

That's enough to cover "always-on" electrical appliances such as fridges and devices left on standby. The government says it should power about a fifth of the average household's electricity use while the sun is shining.

Other essentials, such as the kettle which needs 3 kilowatts of electricity, will be powered through a mix of the 800 watts flowing from the panel with the rest coming from the national grid.

British Gas said plug-in panels won't solely power a home but can "meaningfully reduce how much electricity you need to buy during the daytime".

Government tests found sample systems could operate with no unacceptable heating or unsafe energy flows.

Each device comes with a microinverter which constantly monitors the connection to the grid.

If the electricity cuts out, from a power cut for example, or if the panel is simply unplugged, the microinverter senses that and shuts down in milliseconds so it can never push live electricity into dead wiring.

To be legally sold in Great Britain, new panels must be tested against the industry's G98 standard and the government's product specification.

If a panel meets these requirements, it will appear as compliant on the Energy Networks Association's public register, external, so it is definitely worth checking before buying.

The panels will come with a mounting kit and instructions. Tools may be needed but professional installation isn't required.

Once mounted, connect the microinverter and plug into a mains socket - ideally a external socket that is weatherproof.

They aren't permanently attached so they can be moved to a different property.

People may need permission from their landlord, freeholder or building owner.

Households will need to let the electricity Distribution Network Operator (DNO) know within 28 days of plugging the panel in. This is the company that owns the cables in the area, not your energy provider.

Find them by using National Grid's postcode tool., external

BreakingNewsTab.title: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Massive landslides and flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have caused widespread damage and left hundreds dead or missing.

Search and rescue operations are under way. Chinese state media has said there are significant casualties, while Nepalese officials anticipate "huge scale loss".

Here is what we know so far.

"Additional analysis of nearby seismic stations, long period seismic waves, and satellite imagery led to the determination that the seismic event was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow, and that no earthquake had occurred," USGS said on Thursday.

Earlier Nepali authorities had also told the BBC that a massive chunk of ice may have collapsed from a mountain, pulling down rocks and other sediments with it.

Climate change is known to be driving faster glacier melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region and, as rescue efforts continue, scientists are trying to piece together the exact order of events.

Simon Cook, senior lecturer in energy environment and security at the University of Dundee who specialises in glaciology, said "climate change could have an impact".

He told the BBC "permafrost is partially holding some mountainsides together, this permafrost is warming and thawing and degrading so you are going to get more landslides".

One possibility is that water from rainfall or melting ice may have destabilised the ground or ice, triggering a chain reaction.

Scientist will be looking at satellite images of exactly where the landslide occurred, whether any glacial lakes suddenly drained, and where the river might have become blocked, as well as data on recent rainfall.

A deluge of material careered towards northern Nepalese towns, including areas popular with mountaineering tourists and pilgrims. The border is around 40 miles (64.4km) north of Nepal's capital city Kathmandu.

Footage showed a wall of mud and rock sweeping away buildings, roads and vehicles, as people fled the fast-moving wave of material in the Nuwakot region.

In one video, a towering wall of water and mud was seen rushing down a gorge along the Trishuli River and enveloping the Rasuvagadhi Border check point, a multi-storey building.

Severe flooding has been reported along the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers.

Deaths have also been reported in villages on the Tibetan side of the border.

The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIDMOD) has warned secondary flooding could occur in the coming days as a result of the debris that washed into the river systems.

In a report, the ICIDMOD said they are in the process of assessing whether the Trishuli River has been temporarily blocked in narrow sections. If it has been blocked, it is at risk of forming a landslide dam - and a second flooding event.

Authorities and scientists are continuing to evaluate the size, location and stability of any potential blockages.

Nepal's prime minister said "the entire nation has been left shocked and deeply distressed" and that officials would coordinate with China on the response.

China's President Xi Jinping urged an "all-out" search effort, and promised stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary impacts.

In neighbouring India, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said his government was "prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance".

UN Secretary General António Guterres says he is "saddened by the severe flooding", adding that UN teams and partners are mobilising supplies and personnel in Nepal to support the government-led response.

The US has promised $500,000 (£367,982) in aid which will be used to cover emergency shelter, water, sanitation and other relief items for communities affected by the floods.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the British government would do "everything we can" to support British nationals in Nepal.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Teenagers, 13 and 14, among 33 UK nationals missing in Nepal floods
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Thirty-three people from the UK, including a 13-year-old girl and 14-year-old boy, are among hundreds missing following a deadly flash flood near the Nepal-Tibet border.

Nepali police said 177 bodies had now been recovered from affected areas, and that 33 people were receiving treatment.

Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said that 826 people are missing, with the Nepal Tourism Board saying 644 tourists are out of contact.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he is in touch with local authorities and "will do everything we can" to support British nationals, urging those in the region "to follow guidance from the local authorities and follow our travel advice".

The UK Foreign Office said it is working closely with Nepalese authorities "following concerning reports of British nationals who are missing" and has encouraged Brits to follow local guidance and "remain alert to the changing situation".

According to police, 113 of the missing tourists are Nepalese, and 54 are from the US.

Excursion company Alpine Eco Trek, which offers guided expeditions and tours in Nepal, confirmed to the BBC that it has not been able to establish contact with a group of 12 Britons who were booked on a tour to Mount Kailash, and were in the region when the flash floods struck.

According to the company's travel logs, shared with the Press Association, the age of the missing British citizens ranges from 13 to 65.

It said the youngest member of the group was a 13-year-old girl.

The company said it had made attempts to charter a rescue helicopter but were unable to fly due to poor conditions, and will continue to help with ongoing rescue efforts on Thursday.

It also reported four of the firm's Nepali tour guides are also missing.

The company's manager Kumar Adhikari said he was in contact with the guides until 08:40 when they were expected to be at Tibet's immigration office, but their phones were disconnected.

"We were hoping that inside it was safe," he told PA, "but later the video came from China's government which [showed] even Tibet's side was hit by the flood."

Adhikari said he was "slowly responding to" the families of the Britons but has been unable to give them any updates, adding he has been in contact with the British consulate and forwarded them copies of the clients' passports.

"I feel so sad. We are just thinking about what to do next...We are in pain at the moment, deep pain."

Other tour companies have also been impacted by the flash floods, with British citizens among other tours being affected.

The Trekkers' Society, which organises tours in Nepal, Tibet, and Bhutan, said nine UK nationals on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash are missing after they crossed the Nepal-Tibet border.

It said four males, aged between 14 and 50, and five females aged 40 - 53 remained unaccounted for.

The society's general manager said the group were at Chinese immigration at the border when the flood happened, but it has no contact with the tour guide since.

Himalayan Glacier US told the BBC they have lost contact with a group of 47 guests and staff who where making a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, which included two British citizens.

Kailash Journeys also reported a group of 27 guests and staff missing, with a spokesperson saying they were last in contact with them early Wednesday morning local time.

A list of names provided to the BBC included two men who are British citizens.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he is "deeply concerned" by news of the flash flooding, and wrote on social media: "All my thoughts are with those affected and with British nationals in the area and their relatives here at home".

In a joint statement with Australia, the EU, Finland, France, Norway and Switzerland, the UK embassy in Nepal urged British nationals in Nepal to "exercise caution in affected areas".

The flood hit early on Wednesday in Rasuwa, just north of Nepal's capital Kathmandu.

Preliminary information suggested it was caused by an earthquake, but the US Geological Survey said additional analysis indicated "the seismic energy was instead generated by a landslide."

It said a magnitude 5.2 seismic event caused by a "glacial collapse and debris flow" occurred near the border at 08:37 local time on Wednesday.

Dramatic CCTV footage showed a wall of water and mud hitting buildings near a border crossing and video filmed from inside a bus in Trishuli captured dozens of people trying to flee a flood surge that was surging through the valley.

Meanwhile Chinese state media outlet CCTV said a mudslide in Tibet's Gyirong killed three people and left 265 missing, with rescue efforts under way.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Why Tesla has been caught up in a massive car recall in China
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Hidden car door handles - the sleek designs often found on electric vehicles (EVs) - have come under the spotlight over the past week.

That's after China announced its biggest ever recall of cars, with more than four million vehicles - mostly Teslas - affected.

The recall comes ahead of new regulations in China, requiring cars to have a mechanical release both on the inside and outside of their doors.

Popularised by Elon Musk's electric vehicle giant, this type of handle has become commonplace around the world.

But several incidents have raised concerns that this design may make doors difficult to open in an emergency.

Hidden door handles are widely used in modern cars in China, with around 60% of the top 100 best-selling new energy vehicles, including EVs and hybrids, having them.

The minimalist design gives vehicles a "sleek look and reduces wind drag" but can be confusing to use, car industry analyst Stephen Dyer from consultancy AlixPartners told the BBC.

"Even I often find it difficult to locate the switch to open the door from the inside of an unfamiliar vehicle," said Dyer, who is based in Shanghai.

But beyond their usability, the handles have been blamed for endangering the lives of drivers and passengers.

Electronically powered door handles became an industry trend, but raised "real safety concerns" when doors failed to open promptly, delaying rescue efforts after accidents, said Nanyang Technological University associate professor Lyu Chen.

"A door handle may seem simple, but it becomes safety-critical in the seconds after a crash," Chen said.

Chinese carmaker Xiaomi faced intense scrutiny following two fatal crashes in 2025 involving its SU7 model, when suspected electrical failures allegedly trapped occupants.

One of the incidents took place on a highway in Tongling city, eastern China, killing three people, according to regional news coverage cited by state-controlled media Global Times.

Relatives of the victims said the passengers were stuck in the car as the vehicle's doors could not be unlocked after the collision, the outlet said.

At the time, Xiaomi's representatives said the SU7 had mechanical emergency release handles that function even without power, which are located at the bottom of each door.

The company added at the time that it was investigating the matter and cooperating with the police.

The latest models of the SU7 come with new door handles that can be opened without power.

Xiaomi has not responded to BBC requests for comment.

Tesla has also faced lawsuits in the US over its door handle designs.

The company has been sued by the only survivor of a crash in 2024 involving a Cybertruck - Tesla's electric pickup - that killed three college students in California.

Survivor Jordan Miller alleged that the Cybertruck's design trapped passengers in the burning vehicle and blocked their rescue.

The car did not have door handles and the electronic buttons meant to open the doors failed to work, according to his lawyers from The Veen Firm.

"When you design a vehicle with no mechanical way to open the doors from the outside, you are betting the electronics will work in every scenario, including a high-speed crash followed by a fire," said one of the lawyers in a statement.

In court filings, Tesla denied any wrongdoing and said the Cybertruck is compliant with US federal safety standards, the Guardian reported.

There have been other cases in the US of passengers, including children, allegedly being trapped in Tesla cars after the doors suddenly stopped working.

The BBC has contacted Tesla for comment.

In February, China said it would ban hidden door handles, making it the first country to do so.

The new rules, which take effect on 1 January 2027, mean new car designs without physical release mechanisms on the inside and outside of their doors cannot be sold.

The cars' interior must also carry signs to show how to open the door.

The measures in China come ahead of the US and European Union, which typically lead regulations around road safety and emissions, Dyer noted.

One reason is likely to be the sheer number of EVs in China, he added.

On 21 August, China's State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) announced that Tesla and some major Chinese car makers - including Xiaomi, XPeng and Geely - would recall more than four million vehicles.

Some engineers say the measures may not go far enough to resolve safety concerns.

Engineering instructor Lim Hong Wee said the measures do not address the need for a mechanical way to open the doors.

Access to a car during an emergency should not depend on software, said Lim from the National University of Singapore.

The measures mainly address the issue of people being able to get out of a vehicle, but do not provide a reliable way for rescuers to get in, said Gokul Krithivasan from risk management consultancy SecureSafe.

Warning labels are also a "weak remedy", he added. "When panicked, people fall back on their instinctive responses, and don't read small print in a dark and possibly smoke-filled cabin."

For now, it is unclear whether there will be similar recalls outside China.

The BBC understands that carmakers have not yet notified authorities of any plans for a similar recall in the US.

The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration told the BBC that it is reviewing whether it will require emergency door-exit systems in vehicles.

In Europe, regulators have flagged the potential hazards related to hidden handles and drafted new standards to ensure they still work even if a car's power is cut off.

Engineering lecturer Lyu Chen said that while concealed door handles are still common in EV designs, manufacturers and regulators are paying increasing attention to how they design their doors.

Since cars are built to sell globally, it is likely that the safety requirements in China will be adopted elsewhere, he added.

"The common principle is clear: emergency entry and exit should remain possible even after a loss of electrical power."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Pakistan PIMS fire: Witnesses say door was locked as Islamabad hospital blaze killed 14 babies
BreakingNewsTab.text:
It was just after dawn on Wednesday morning at a maternity ward in the Pakistani capital when a horrific blaze erupted.

It would go on to kill 14 infants as parents say they waited hours for help to arrive.

Hivsa Walid was near the room at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital with her sister-in-law, who had given birth days earlier. She initially heard a shout and thought a patient had died - but then she saw smoke.

The pair fled with the baby, who is so small she does not yet have a name.

"We didn't even think about our belongings. We just grabbed the baby and rushed downstairs.

"Some patients had delivered their babies just that night. I don't even know how we managed to get down - it was all a blur."

The fire broke out in an air-conditioning unit on the third floor of the mother and child unit at PIMS, one of the main state-run hospitals in Islamabad. Only one of the 15 babies present was saved.

Khurram Mehmood, 40, told AFP news agency there was a long wait for rescue workers. "I lost my daughter. She was only three days old," he said.

Jaweria, the mother of another victim, told AFP news agency the door to the maternity ward was locked.

"For two hours I kept crying and wailing," she said. "Police arrived after four hours and said they are here to investigate."

"Why did the doctors leave the children there?" she asks.

"To hell with you, rescue team and police. Babies burnt to death there, but nobody could save them."

Rana Imran Sikander, the hospital's executive director, told the BBC the ward's door was not locked but was manned. He cited the need to protect babies from being stolen, something that has happened before at government hospitals.

Walid suggested PIMS's safety protocols were inadequate, despite it being a major hospital. "There should have been fire extinguishers and protocols, but no one was doing anything - everyone was just running."

The father of a baby who died told Reuters he had been visiting the ward for eight days and the building had "no fire security, no proper exits".

"All doors were closed, only one door was for us to visit our children. They kept the other doors locked because they feared we would come to see our children too often."

Several eyewitnesses have claimed duty staff were not around.

People had to "break the door down" and rescue teams were forced to smash the windows to control the flames, a witness who did not give her name told AFP.

Abdul Ghafoor, another witness, told AFP he tried to get into the building to rescue patients but couldn't reach the maternity ward.

"There was thick black smoke inside and patients were trapped," he said. "Rescue teams arrived after almost two hours."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Trump officials threaten Kennedy Center demolition if court blocks renovations
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The Trump administration has threatened to demolish the Kennedy Center if planned renovations for the performing arts venue are not allowed to be carried out, court documents show.

Attorneys from the justice department have also asked for President Donald Trump's name to be put back on the building after it was removed in June following a court order.

"An order blocking the Board from appropriately recognising President Trump," the lawyers argued, "will cause donors to flee, financial contributions to dry up, and structural rehabilitation to stop".

The venue has been among the storied sites in Washington that Trump has sought to renovate since he returned to the White House in 2025.

Trump's lawyers have argued that without the renovations the venue "will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down".

They also called the venue "embarrassing to the Nation's Capital".

After the "decrepit structure" is taken down, justice department attorney Brantley Mayers wrote, a determination of what to build on the site will follow, including the option of a large outdoor amphitheatre overlooking the Potomac River.

The threat to demolish the building comes just weeks after the Kennedy Center board voted to add Trump's name back to the facade of the venue and to proceed with a two-year closure for proposed renovations.

Many of the board members who voted are Trump allies who were appointed by the president.

In late May, a US judge ruled that the president's name had been added to the venue unlawfully, as it cannot be renamed without congressional approval.

The judge ordered that the name be removed, and so it was taken down in June.

The case stemmed from a broader legal dispute over the renaming of the cultural institution, which US law designates as a memorial to President John F Kennedy.

It is the latest in series of projects that Trump has taken on since returning to Washington.

BreakingNewsTab.title: At least 12 dead as wildfires sweep through northern Algeria
BreakingNewsTab.text:
At least 12 people have been killed and dozens injured as wildfires burn through large swathes of northern Algeria.

Civil protection authorities said dozens of blazes swept through several provinces along the country's northern coastline.

At least 54 people had suffered burn injuries, with at least six of them being treated in intensive care, Interior Minister Said Sayoud said on Wednesday night.

The deaths comes as northern Africa swelters under a severe heatwave, with Tunisia and Algeria particularly affected.

Sayoud said five people were killed in Jijel province, four in Bejaia and three in Tizi Ouzou.

He has travelled to Bejaia with the Algerian Health Minister Mohamed Seddik Ait Messaoudene to "assess" local firefighting and evacuation efforts, government officials said.

Many homes in Bejaia and Jijel have been evacuated, according to the civil protection agency and local media.

Footage shared by local broadcaster Jijel News showed residents taking refuge in a post office as thick clouds of smoke billowed around them.

Firefighters were battling 69 blazes across the country, the civil protection agency said earlier on Wednesday evening.

The Bejaia region saw devastating fires tear through forest and farmland three years ago when 30 people were killed.

Last month, the authorities recorded at least six deaths caused by fires, with crews battling more than 2,000 blazes across Algeria in July alone.

While Algeria regularly experiences forest fires around the summer months, climate change has exacerbated the intensity and severity of recent wildfires in the country.

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said extreme heat had become common in North Africa, a region that has seen the most rapid warming of the six subregions of Africa - 0.43C per decade - between 1991 and 2025.

Rising heat and water shortages have also led to an increase in camel deaths during summer heatwaves in Algeria, a recent study revealed.

FinanceTab.title: Experts' five tips to make a rented property feel like home
FinanceTab.text:
It can be a balancing act making a rented property feel like your own.

You want somewhere that feels warm and personal but without spending a fortune changing a flat or house owned by someone else and making alterations that put a deposit at risk.

Higher average mortgage rates and hefty deposits mean buying a home is out of reach for many, who are renting for longer.

The good news is that transforming a rental doesn't have to mean a major renovation.

With a free weekend, a relatively small budget and a few clever changes, even a bland or tired-looking place can be spruced-up.

We asked B&Q chief executive Graham Bell and interior designers Lara Clarke and Lydia Lloyd for their top tips that won't break the bank or annoy a landlord.

Before making anything permanent, check what your tenancy agreement allows.

Bell, of DIY chain B&Q, says many landlords may be open to sensible improvements, particularly where something is being upgraded rather than fundamentally changed.

But getting permission first avoids an expensive argument when you move out.

Bell also says it is important to take time to prepare properly.

"The biggest mistake is that people don't plan enough," he says. "It's all the planning that goes into it that's important, making sure you have everything.

"My dad would tell me to always measure twice and cut once."

He recommends deciding exactly what you want to achieve, measuring the space and buying everything you need before you start.

Online tutorials can also help with relatively simple DIY projects.

If you don't want to spend money improving someone else's property, focus on temporary changes that can come with you when you move.

Bell recommends renter-friendly products such as stick-on tiles for the kitchen, suction storage products in the bathroom and expandable blinds that can be fitted without drilling.

Interior designer Clarke says artwork is probably the easiest way to make a rental feel more homely because it "instantly makes a space feel more occupied and finished".

She suggests looking for affordable vintage oil paintings, exhibition posters or framed sketches at antique markets, then securing them with command strips so they can be removed without leaving holes in the plaster.

Lighting is one of the quickest ways to transform a space.

Bell says rentals often come with "bright, bright lights", but swapping them out for something warmer can dramatically change the atmosphere of a room.

He suggests experimenting using lightbulbs or strip lighting with different tones. Strip lighting is often found in kitchens but a softer glow can change the whole feel of the space without requiring a major renovation.

Rather than depending on a single overhead light, Clarke recommends building up different sources from around the room.

"Mood lighting really helps make a space feel more cosy and homely," she says.

"Add table and floor lamps too and there are plenty of battery-powered options around now so you don't have to worry about finding a plug socket."

Clarke says the effect can be made even cosier by pairing lighting with soft furnishings, such as floor-to-ceiling curtains and scatter cushions in different colours and patterns.

Lloyd believes scent is a "simple but powerful way to make a home feel inviting".

Buying candles, diffusers and room sprays "can help create a warm, cosy atmosphere, especially as we move into the colder months".

She recommends fragrances such as sandalwood, cedarwood, cinnamon and cardamom as they "are perfect for bringing a sense of comfort into the home".

She also suggests "adding layers of texture through cushions, throws and blankets" thinking about mixing materials like velvet, boucle or chunky knits.

FinanceTab.title: Six essential skills employers say job seekers should have to stand out
FinanceTab.text:
The ability to communicate, collaborate and solve problems are among skills that employers say they are looking for in potential job hires.

In a major five-year study, the National Foundation for Educational Research (NFER) identified six key transferable skills that will count as much as qualifications in getting and keeping a job in the coming decade.

It comes as NFER research, published last year, external, suggests it may become even harder to find a job as AI and automation could see up to three million low- to mid-level jobs disappearing by 2035.

As more than one million young people are not in education, employment or training - the highest level in over a decade - we have been speaking to businesses about how people can demonstrate the key skills employers are looking for.

One of the big shocks for many leaving education and trying to get into work is the sudden lack of structure, so being able to prioritise your own work is seen by many employers as essential.

In Leeds, Christian Townsley, the co-founder of the North Bar group, says working in a busy bar is all about staying calm and keeping a "cool head".

"It's important that you can organise, you can multitask, you can identify who's next at the bar and remember that," he says.

Townsley offers trial shifts as part of the recruitment process, to give job seekers an opportunity to showcase these skills in action.

"We'll observe them working with customers, working with the team, seeing how they fit in, seeing how they communicate," he says.

As people get promoted, they are expected to take on more responsibilities and be able to manage them within the role.

"There's organisation, ordering beer, pricing beer, planning social media, marketing, recruiting," Townsley adds.

Many employers want new recruits to be able to react to issues as they arise and take decisive action.

Maria Aderonmu went from a political science degree to a career at Morgan Sindall Infrastructure, a company that delivers infrastructure projects across energy, defence, rail and more in the UK.

Now working in strategy, Aderonmu often has to think on the go and says "adapting to each kind of situation" has been one of the biggest things she's learnt through work.

At university, she was involved in the debating society and now realises that has prepared her for thinking on her feet.

People director India Chaplin says she doesn't expect "every young person to have come across every scenario".

Her tip is to think about how your experiences of solving problems outside of work - at school, say, or when you have been part of a team - could apply to a work setting.

"There's lots of different ways that people can show the softer skills that we're looking for and how they would approach a problem, even if it was a scenario they've maybe not come across to help think how they would put that into practice in the working environment."

At Barbour's factory in South Shields, HR director Lynn Bassett says being able to collaborate is something they look for in everyone they recruit.

"Each department is interlinked with one another so working as one team is really important," she says.

Bassett says what they are looking for when hiring is how people can talk about their own experiences of collaboration.

"They might not have the specific experience that's needed for the role, but we look more at those transferable skills."

Jude Hillary, the economist who led the project for NFER, says these human skills are what will allow people to get into and keep work at a higher skill level, even while automation bites.

"This is where the job growth is going to be in the labour market," he says. "It's really important young people come into the labour market being able to compete for these jobs."

And he believes focusing on these six essential employment skills will help young people adapt in a time of huge change.

"It's increasingly likely that during the course of your working life, you might have to make some fairly dramatic changes in what you're doing as your job gets replaced by technology."

An independent review led by Alan Milburn, a former health secretary, has been looking at the scale of young people not working, learning or training.

The interim report said 42% of employers listed a lack of soft skills or work readiness as a challenge when hiring young people. Only 10% cited the resilience of young people which was the next biggest concern.

There is increasing pressure for schools, colleges and universities to focus on giving young people what they need to be work-ready alongside academic learning.

Already, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has signalled that more teenagers should start technical education at 14 and has supported a work experience scheme for 10,000 young people announced this week by the retail chain Sainsbury's.

In September, the final report of the Milburn review is expected to set out its proposals on how to get more young adults into secure work.

Additional reporting by Hannah Karpel.

FinanceTab.title: Household energy bills to hit three-year high as Ofgem announces 4% rise from October
FinanceTab.text:
Energy prices for millions of households will rise to the highest level for three years, under regulator Ofgem's price cap.

Ofgem said the price cap will increase by 4% on 1 October, driven by higher wholesale gas prices due to the Iran war.

A household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay £60 a year more, but more than a third of households are on fixed tariffs so their prices will not change.

The government said its cut to VAT on electricity bills will save households £45 and it was doing more to address cost of living pressures, but opposition parties said Labour was not doing enough.

The new cap will hit household bills as the colder weather arrives in October.

Suppliers say energy debt has rocketed and, with high bills likely to persist, have called for more support for those struggling to pay.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham acknowledged people would find the increase "difficult" but highlighted his move to cut VAT from electricity bills, which he said would help from October.

He said the government would "continue to look... at how we get energy prices down in the long term".

As well as the VAT cut, the government said the warm homes discount would take £150 off bills for six million households this winter.

But analysts at the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight have forecast domestic energy prices may rise a further 9% in the new year, bringing renewed concern to households during the coldest months.

Shadow energy secretary Claire Coutinho said the government must "put cheap energy first", saying while it had promised to cut bills by £300 they had "gone up by nearly £400 instead".

Liberal Democrat spokesperson for energy and net zero Pippa Heylings said Burnham needed to "wake up to the scale of the challenge" and make bold changes to lower bills.

Reform UK treasury spokesperson Robert Jenrick said households faced a "difficult period ahead" and said Labour's "net zero ideology" is driving up bills.

Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown also weighed in, saying the government should introduce a "machine gaming tax" and use proceeds to help those struggling with bills.

Longer term, he said Burnham should look at a social tariff for energy.

"I think Andy Burnham, I know him well, will want to do something along the lines I'm suggesting," he said.

Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said while gas bills were rising by 8%, electricity bills were actually falling slightly due to the government's VAT cut.

He said the gap between gas and electricity bills meant it would be cheaper for households to transition to heat pumps.

Around 35% of households - or 11 million households - are on fixed tariffs, but 22 million in England, Wales and Scotland are on tariffs affected by the price cap.

Ofgem said the price cap will rise by £60 per year – or £5 per month – to £1,723 for the typical household using both electricity and gas and paying by direct debit if this level was sustained for a year.

Kenward told the Today programme the rise was technically 3.6%, but Ofgem always rounds the number which is why it publicised the 4% figure.

Kenward added: "Savings are available by choosing a fixed tariff, which are available at £100 or more below the October price cap."

The energy cap sets a maximum price for each unit of gas and electricity, not the total bill, so a household's final bill depends on their usage.

In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back owing to high prices of recent years while energy efficiency has improved.

Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year.

The price rise has been driven by wholesale costs, which make up just over a third of a domestic dual-fuel energy bill.

The average price of gas has been 61% higher over the past three months compared to late 2025, according to suppliers' trade body Energy UK.

And households are still paying hundreds of pounds a year more on average than before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 started the energy crisis. Bills have gone up by about 70% compared with the pre-crisis norm, according to industry data.

That means unpaid bills and charges have shot up. Energy UK estimates total debt to have collectively risen to £6bn, with an expectation it will increase to about £7bn by the end of the year.

The trade body has called for a flexible discounted tariff for those most in need, funded by taxation. That is supported by many debt charities.

Vanessa Northam, director at debt charity StepChange, said the increasing number of people seeking help often had high energy debt, averaging at £2,600 on top of other financial commitments.

The charity has joined calls for the government to introduce a social tariff.

Her advice for those who might only just be managing as winter approaches includes:

Taking stock of all household money coming in and going out

Look closely at how much energy you are using, and be alert if there are a series of estimated bills, which might prove to be inaccurate

Telling your supplier if you think you are going to struggle

Some information is available online, but it is often best to try to talk to someone who can fully understand your situation

Suppliers offer various support schemes to anyone struggling to pay, or who is likely to find it difficult.

Energy UK has a list of these schemes, external. But it stresses companies can often only help if you tell your supplier you are unable to pay.

FinanceTab.title: Back to school: How parents can save on uniform costs
FinanceTab.text:
Back to school can stir up many emotions for parents, including anxiety about the extra costs it brings.

Almost half of parents said they're worried about the cost of school uniforms, according to research by the charity Save the Children and the Baby Bank Alliance network.

And a third of the 2,000 parents polled said they've sacrificed things for themselves to meet back-to-school costs like uniforms, bags or books.

New rules limiting the number of items branded with a school logo to three per child come into force in September, aimed at helping ease the financial burden.

From baby banks to council grants, here are ways parents can ease the cost of kitting out their kids for school.

Save the Children said the new uniform rules are a "good start" but back-to-school costs remain a concern for families across almost all income brackets.

The government said schools should make second-hand uniforms accessible to parents.

"Speak to a teacher you trust, and explain that the costs are difficult," said Megan Meek-O'Connor, head of England and Westminster at Save the Children.

Many schools have uniform hubs, swap shops and sales just before term starts, and hardship funds.

In London, the School Uniform Reuse Network launched earlier this year, giving schools practical advice to start or improve their own swap shops.

During its first term of operation, it saw more than 1,500 items reused across 24 schools.

Parents of older children may not realise a so-called baby bank can help them, but many of the 400 support hubs across the UK provide uniforms for children up to and through secondary school.

In its latest survey of members, the Baby Bank Alliance found school uniform was reported as a priority item for the first time.

Late summer is one of the busiest times for Little Stars Shrewsbury - just over half the children helped since June have been given uniform support.

Hannah Stoddart, operations manager at Little Stars Shrewsbury, said families come to them in varying circumstances. A child starting school might need fully kitting out, while an older pupil may just need to replace one or two items.

Stoddart stressed that while the summer holidays "take their toll", the charity provides help all year.

"So when they've had that growth spurt, when they've scuffed their shoes or they've ripped their trousers or they need a winter coat, that's something they can come back to us for as well," she said.

You may be able to get a grant from your local authority if your income is below a certain threshold or you're receiving certain benefits.

These can be worth up to £200 per child.

Eligibility and how much you can get can vary according to where in the UK you live, so it is best to check with your council directly.

Struggling with uniform costs is common and people shouldn't feel ashamed if they need to ask for help, said Meek-O'Connor.

"Uniform is supposed to be about making school kind of more accessible, more equal... it should be something positive," she said.

FinanceTab.title: Reform proposes £30 tax rebate for HMRC phone delays
FinanceTab.text:
People on hold to HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) for more than 30 minutes would get £30 off their tax bill under a Reform UK government, Robert Jenrick has announced.

Reform's economy spokesman said HMRC's treatment of taxpayers was "offensive to working people" and his party would tie the pay of senior HMRC officials to customer service targets.

To prevent abuse, the tax credit for phone delays would be limited to two occasions in a given tax year, Jenrick said.

HMRC said its customer service had "vastly" improved over the past two years, with average call waiting times now 11 minutes and more of its services being delivered online or through its app.

In January 2025, the Public Accounts committee accused HMRC of seeking to "degrade its telephone service to drive taxpayers to digital channels" in a highly critical report., external

The MPs' report said nearly 44,000 customers were cut off without warning after being on hold for more than an hour in 2024 and "HMRC's treatment of taxpayers has damaged trust in the tax system".

Jenrick highlighted the findings - which were rejected as "completely baseless" by the then boss of HMRC - at a media conference in central London.

"Frankly, it is offensive to working people and I have had enough," said the former Tory MP.

"So, we will give HMRC a big incentive to actually provide proper customer service.

"I'm announcing today that under a Reform government, if you spend more than half an hour waiting for HMRC to answer your call, you will get a £30 credit off your tax bill. If HMRC delay, they can repay.

"And to make sure that the staff actually hit their targets, we'll tie the pay of senior HMRC officials to their customer service performance."

The HMRC said 80% of customer interactions now took place digitally, reducing the time spent on the phone to advisers, who were there to deal with vulnerable or digitally excluded customers or those with particularly complex problems.

A spokesperson said: "Our customer service performance has improved significantly with average call wait times now around 11 minutes.

"Overall customer satisfaction is at around 80% with more people than ever using our digital services, including millions using the HMRC app."

Jenrick also pledged to scrap UK privacy rules in favour of a "light-touch" approach to data protection as part of a bid to slash "red tape" for businesses if Reform wins power.

He said the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which mirrors EU legislation and was adopted as domestic law after Brexit, had "strangled" tech firms and small enterprises.

The framework would be replaced by rules modelled on New Zealand's privacy legislation, which Reform says has the lightest-touch regime still recognised as being "adequate" by the EU.

Labour accused Reform of wanting to "scrap vital safeguards that protect people's private data" with its "unworkable and unserious plans".
