articles.title: Susan Sarandon leads tributes to Rocky Horror Picture Show co-star Tim Curry
articles.text:
Stars of stage and screen have paid tribute to cult British actor Tim Curry, who has died at the age of 80.

"What I loved about him most was his heart," said Oscar-winner Susan Sarandon, who co-starred with him in The Rocky Horror Picture Show.

Curry, who was born in the north-western English town of Warrington in 1946, passed away peacefully at his home in Los Angeles on Tuesday, said his manager. He had used a wheelchair since suffering a major stroke in 2012.

In a career spanning six decades, the prolific actor left his mark on both theatre and film, ranging from Home Alone 2 and Annie to Stephen King's It and The Hunt for Red October.

But he was perhaps best known for his zany role as the cross-dressing Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show.

He first played the part on stage before the movie adaptation that propelled him to cult stardom.

Sarandon, who played the heroine Janet Weiss in the movie, praised Curry as "a funny, sexy, original".

"Thank you Tim for meaning so much to so many people."

Curry's longtime manager and friend Marcia Hurwitz confirmed he "passed away peacefully at his home in Toluca Lake, Los Angeles on August 25".

Australian actress Nell Campbell, who starred alongside Curry in The Rocky Horror Picture Show, told the BBC: "I feel like the head of our family has just died because he was the head of the Rocky Horror family."

Welsh actor Luke Evans, who played Frank-N-Furter in a Broadway revival, called Curry "a force, a bright fierce flame, an exquisite charm".

In a letter he recently wrote to Curry, Evans thanked him for his fearlessness and for "creating something so enduring, and for inspiring generations of actors to be a little braver than they thought they could be".

The official Rocky Horror Picture Show on Broadway account similarly thanked the late actor for "giving the world a little more freedom, a little more fearlessness, and through the tears in our eyes, the courage to BE IT" - a nod to Curry's delivery of the famous line from the musical: "Don't dream it, be it."

In a statement to Entertainment Weekly, writer and composer Richard O'Brien, who co-wrote the musical and film, remembered the actor as "a wonderful man by nature who was also a wonderful performer".

"He never sought attention and never put himself before the roles that he played," O'Brien said. "He was, in short, a good egg and class act."

Clue co-star and Better Call Saul actor Michael McKean said on social media that his last conversation with Curry was about "life and love and laughter".

"The grim physical state he found himself in has now ended, a blessing. Our blessing was that we had Tim Curry in our lives. RIP, my friend," he wrote.

Two other stars of Clue, where Curry played a butler, Christopher Lloyd and Lesley Ann Warren, also paid tribute on social media.

Lloyd shared a photo of Curry from the film along with a heart emoji and Warren called Curry a "dear companion in crime".

"The brilliant, hilarious, hysterically funny, magician of artistry has left us," she said.

"What an unbelievable joy to have shared a soundstage with him and to engage with such a master talent. I adored him. Bless his wild and inspired soul."

articles.title: How Dolly Parton's business acumen helped her succeed far beyond the charts
articles.text:
Not many musicians would snub a chance to work with Elvis Presley. But when Dolly Parton did so, it made her millions.

In 1974, after writing and recording I Will Always Love You, Parton was asked if Presley could cover the song. She turned him down after his manager demanded half the rights.

"Of course, I cried all night about that," she later said of the ordeal in an interview.

But she wasn't crying in 1992 when Whitney Houston's power-ballad cover became a hit. Global sales of the song topped 20 million, earning Parton more than $10m in royalties, according to business magazine Forbes.

This is the less well-known side of Parton. While country music and films brought her fame, her entrepreneurial zeal brought her fortune.

The country icon signed deals, started companies, and invested in ideas that Forbes says built her a net worth of $450m by the time she died.

Parton wasn't always wealthy. She grew up in poverty and in her 1971 hit Coat of Many Colours describes how she would wear rags to school which her "mama" had knitted together.

In a 2017 BBC interview, she said her father gave her business lessons from early in her career.

"My dad wasn't an educated man, he wasn't able to read and write, but my daddy had a great sense of business," she told the BBC's World Service in 2017.

"So when I got into the music business, I thought of it as a business. And so I started early on keeping my own songs and my own publishing company."

While her publishing company helped build her wealth, Parton had plenty of other business ideas.

In 1985, she co-founded a film and TV production company called Sandollar Productions, which helped to make 90s cult thriller Buffy The Vampire Slayer.

Then there was Dollywood - the theme park in in the foothills of the Smoky Mountains in her home state of Tennessee, which she became co-owner of in 1986. It had changed owners multiple times since it was first set up 25 years earlier and her buy-in exponentially boosted visitor numbers.

She kept improving the park. In 2015, she opened the DreamMore Resort, a four-star hotel and spa down the road from Dollywood. Today, many of Parton's family members work at the theme park and it is the biggest employer in its county.

She launched the Dolly Beauty cosmetics line in 2025 and she opened Dolly's Tennessean Travel Stop in June this year. The shop offers a signature coffee brand named Cup of Ambition, a nod to her Grammy-winning single 9 to 5.

Paul Milliken, a reporter from Fox 5 Atlanta who had interviewed Parton many times, said diversification was the key to her business success.

"It's a lesson that continues from her to this day to young artists," he told BBC's Wake Up to Money.

Parton may have been motivated to make money right into her 80s, but she told the BBC in the 2017 interview that she never lost sight of where she came from.

"Being brought up poor means I don't take things for granted, and no matter how much money I make, I'll always count my blessings quicker and more often than I count my money.

She has "always realised the value of a dollar", too.

"Even now if I go in a store it's hard for me to pay a huge amount of money for one item. I say 'good Lord', what could mummy and daddy have done with that!"

Wealth was more than just a means to an end for Parton. It also allowed her to be generous.

She gave millions away to funding child literacy, providing wildfire relief, and creating a cure for Covid-19. In 2022, she was awarded the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy for her charity work.

Talking about her many business and charity ideas in 2017, she told the BBC: "I just wish I was 30 years old so I could start over again and get all this stuff done... I'm gonna' be working till I fall over bad."

Parton's influence and success depended in part on her role as one of the few things on which Americans could agree.

Parton steadfastly refused to taint her beloved brand by weighing into politics, twice refusing the Presidential Medal of Freedom - having been offered it by Donald Trump and Joe Biden.

Maike Currie, vice president of personal finance at savings firm PensionBee, told the BBC's Wake Up to Money that Parton set examples for others.

Fellow country music megastar Taylor Swift's sound has been compared to Parton musically, but Currie said she may also have taken business inspiration there as well, deciding to rerecord her songs in order to own the rights to them.

Currie described Parton as a "brilliant businesswoman, but also an iconic investor and a real example to women about the power of what happens if women are financially independent".

The star's success tracks with the advice she took from her father, shared with the BBC in her 2017 interview: "He said: 'Don't let other people take advantage of you. You keep your mind on your business'."

Additional reporting by Peter Hoskins, Will Harris and Stephen Ryan

articles.title: Miley Cyrus remembers godmother Dolly Parton as an 'angel by my side'
articles.text:
Miley Cyrus, Taylor Swift, Beyoncé and Sir Paul McCartney have led an outpouring of tributes from celebrities and fans to Dolly Parton following the music icon's death at the age of 80.

Cyrus paid an emotional tribute to her godmother, "Aunt Dolly", describing her as an "angel by my side". She wrote on Instagram, external: "I will always love her and want to make her proud."

The Tennessee-born singer died on Tuesday after "a brief battle with cancer", her team said in a statement.

Parton is known for iconic songs including Jolene, 9 to 5 and I Will Always Love You. She was also a philanthropist, who helped fund one of the first Covid-19 vaccines and poured millions into improving children's literacy.

Miley Cyrus, also born in Tennessee, added: "Our most sacred moments were private and they'll stay there behind the stage, beneath the glamour and between our hearts.

"What I know is Dolly would want me to feel it, write a song about it, and then continue on and be strong."

Her father and Parton's close friend Billy Ray Cyrus remembered the music icon as being "part of our lives, on our TVs, right in our living rooms".

"I have so many moments and memories with Dolly, it's hard to know where to start," he said. "Like every little boy, I grew up loving Dolly Parton."

He recounted a time when he had to apologise to Parton for tabloid rumours which claimed they were having an affair.

"In true Dolly fashion, she just looked at me, winked and said: 'Honey, this trash sells records!'"

Taylor Swift, who began her professional career in country music as a teen in Nashville, paid tribute to Parton's "true grace and true grit, all in one dazzling person".

"A world without Dolly doesn't feel possible, real, or right," the superstar said in a statement. "But because of the eternally generous way she spent her time on this earth and the countless lives she changed for the better, her legacy will be an everlasting one."

As well as "melodies and lyrics she wrote that thawed even the coldest of hearts", Swift acknowledged "the millions of books she provided children all over the world so that they might fall in love with stories the way she did".

She thanked Parton "for the tightropes she walked so that young girls like me could grow up dreaming of joining the circus too".

Sir Paul McCartney reflected on his history with Parton, which began when he met her in Nashville at the Grande Ole Opry just before she started her solo musical career.

"She was so bubbly and full of life, it is difficult to take in the news that she has passed," he said. "Her songwriting, her singing and her philanthropy were unrivaled in the world of country music and it is hard to imagine living in a world without Dolly."

Sir Elton John said he was "shocked and devastated" by the news. "A giant of an artist - unique and irreplaceable, with the kindest heart."

Beyoncé said Parton was the "barometer" and the "North Star".

"Bold and brilliant. Talented and tenacious. You taught so many lessons on how to be uniquely oneself. I am grateful for your art, your heart, your generosity, your humour, your entrepreneurship," she wrote.

Cowboy Carter, Beyoncé's 2024 country album, famously featured a rendition of Parton's song Jolene.

Parton's musical influence spanned generations, and inspired the careers of a fresh wave of female talent.

Sabrina Carpenter, who collaborated with Parton in 2025 on a country-inspired version of Carpenter's hit Please Please Please, posted: "The only thing I could say after we first met was 'she really is an angel walking the earth' and 'we look like we could be sisters!'"

Along with behind the scenes pictures of the pair filming their music video, Carpenter added: "Your light will be something the world will search forever to find again."

Katy Perry, who performed with Parton several times, described her as "a pure, sweet (but not saccharine) sassy, cup of joy".

The singer wrote: "For me, she was an example of a woman who defied the stereotypes for decades. She proved that big boobs, big brains, and a big voice can all exist in one tiny body! But the biggest thing about her by far was her heart."

Stars from across the musical spectrum have shared stories about how important the late singer was to them.

Eminem noted that while he had never met Parton, she made her mark on his life by sending him a note when he was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame calling him "very special".

"I'm sorry we never got a chance to meet, but getting this note from Dolly really had an impact on me. She definitely didn't have to take the time to do it," the rapper said.

"Even for a kid who mostly listened to rap music, she was an icon," he added. "A superstar in every sense. Rest easy Dolly. And thank you for the kind words."

Tributes have also been paid by US presidents past and present.

Donald Trump called her death a "true loss for millions of people", adding: "There has never been anyone like her, and never will."

He ordered American flags across the US to be lowered in her memory - a rare honour that is mostly reserved for elected leaders and other officials in the US government.

"Rest in Peace, Dolly! The World loves you," the US president said.

Former US President Bill Clinton called Parton "one of a kind – a great songwriter and performer who told the stories of everyday Americans with honesty, humility, and heart".

He noted that while her star grew, she "never forgot where she came from" and always gave back through her philanthropic efforts.

And Barack Obama said it was "hard to imagine many people having a bigger impact than Dolly Parton".

In London, Buckingham Palace guards played a military rendition of 9 to 5 in honour of her.

The Royal Family also wrote: "Remembering the late, great Dolly, who brought joy, comfort and inspiration to so many - including the millions of children given free books through her Imagination Library. We will always [heart] you".

Parton had been struggling with health issues recently, which in May saw the superstar cancel a highly anticipated Las Vegas residency that was due to start next month.

At the time, she cited a longtime struggle with kidney stones, and said she had been "responding really well to meds and treatments" and "improving every day."

In typical Dolly style, she joked that she couldn't "be dizzy carrying around banjos, guitars and such on five-inch heels - and you know that I'm going to be wearing them".

Parton has died nearly 18 months after the passing of her husband, Carl Dean. The pair were married for more than 60 years, but he was famously private and rarely seen with her in public. They did not have any children.

She died at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center in Nashville "surrounded by loved ones", her spokesperson said, but did not give details of her condition.

articles.title: Heart, hope and a steely determination: Dolly Parton's musical legacy
articles.text:
In 1980, Dolly Parton was filming her first Hollywood movie, 9 To 5, and between scenes she had an idea for the tune that would become the movie's theme song.

But her guitar was banned from the set - so she made the beat by strumming her acrylic nails together.

The sound, she realised, was just like the typewriter used by her character, a married secretary who is constantly belittled and sexually harassed by her boss.

Excited, she ran over and sang the song to her co-stars Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda, who was also the film's producer.

"Lily and I looked at each other and we had goosebumps," Fonda said. "And we knew, this is not just a movie song, this is an anthem."

Released in November 1980, 9 To 5 became Parton's only US number one as a solo artist, and earned her an Oscar nomination for best song.

She loved to tell the fingernail story, but 9 To 5 has another legacy - for its powerful statements about working life and women's place in the corporate world.

You can probably sing the hook off the top of your head. "Working 9 To 5 / What a way to make a living!" It's jaunty and catchy. The sentiment is universal. Work sucks.

But dig deeper and Dolly's expressing real fury.

"It's a rich man's game, no matter what they call it / And you spend your life putting money in his wallet," she sings. "They just use your mind and they never give you credit."

The lyrics tapped into real frustrations and gave working women a voice.

But there's a reason why you might not have noticed the anger that fuels Dolly's song. She simply doesn't sing it that way - even though she had every right to, having navigated the sexism of the music industry from the age of 13.

Her early breakthrough came in 1967 when she was hired as the "girl singer" on The Porter Wagoner Show, a TV showcase for country singer Porter Wagoner that reached millions of viewers each week.

Together, they released 21 hit duets including Just Someone I Used to Know, If Teardrops Were Pennies and Please Don't Stop Loving Me.

But as Parton's star rose, she began to outshine her co-star. Eventually, she realised she needed to strike out as a solo artist – writing I Will Always Love You as a letter of apology to her former mentor. He responded by suing her for breach of contract in 1979, demanding $3m (£2,2m).

Wanting to avoid a lengthy court battle, Parton settled for about $1m.

"I made up my mind that if he could live with it, I could live without it," she wrote in her autobiography. "I suppose Porter has done all right with it. I am neither his conscience nor his accountant."

It was typical of the star's ability to radiate cheery goodwill that she never held a grudge against Wagoner, always crediting him with giving her a crucial career break, even after their relationship fell apart.

But she was nobody's fool. Take, for example, the battle over the rights to I Will Always Love You.

After it hit number one in the country charts, Elvis Presley called – he loved the song and wanted to record a cover.

"You cannot imagine how excited I am about this," she told him. "This is the greatest thing that's ever happened to me as a songwriter."

But the night before the recording session, his notoriously hard-nosed manager, Colonel Tom Parker, called Parton and told her Elvis wouldn't record the song unless she handed over half of the lucrative publishing rights.

"I said, 'Well, that throws a new light on this. Because I can't give you half the publishing. I'm gonna leave that to my family,'" Parton told Reba McEntire's podcast in 2020.

"And he said, 'Well, then we can't do it.' And I cried all night."

"I mean, it was like the worst thing," she told Country Music Television. "People were saying, 'You're nuts. It's Elvis Presley. Hell, I'd give him all of it.'

"I said, 'I can't.' I always wondered what it would sound like. I know he would have killed it [in a good way]."

But Parton had the last laugh.

When Whitney Houston recorded her blockbuster version of I Will Always Love You for The Bodyguard soundtrack in 1992, the country star still owned the rights and earned "enough money to buy Graceland", Presley's mansion.

Instead, she invested the money in a black neighbourhood in Nashville, Tennessee, saying she thought it was an apt way to honour Houston's legacy.

That determination to stand up for herself, and to value her music as more than just a commodity, is an essential part of Parton's legacy.

Without her example, would Taylor Swift have stood up to the hedge funds who bought her back catalogue, re-recording her biggest hits to rob them of royalties?

Perhaps not – but either way, Dolly approved.

"Smart!" she said when asked about Swift's masterplan. "She's so smart, she's so great, she's genius. I mean really, look at what she's doing! That's amazing!"

Mourning Parton's death, Swift acknowledged the star's "backbone of steel" in the struggle "to defend her own self worth as an artist".

Musically, her legacy is just as profound.

Parton was about six years old when she wrote her first song: Little Tiny Tasseltop, an ode to her favourite doll and its corn-silk hair.

For the rest of her career, she turned everyday details like those into songs of hope and heart.

Her 1971 classic Coat of Many Colors tells the profoundly moving story of Parton as a child being proud of the ragged, hand-sewn clothes her mother had made for her.

The 1974 concept album My Tennessee Mountain Home, meanwhile, is a musical autobiography that opens with Parton reciting the first letter she wrote home after moving to Nashville as a teenager.

"A couple of folks already told me that they might record a couple of my songs, so I'll be makin' enough money to get by," she sang. "And I don't want you to be worrying about me bein' hungry or anything."

The album cover is a photo of the two-room log cabin that was Parton's actual childhood home in the 1940s and 50s, and the rest of the songs paint an idyllic picture of her childhood.

Even when the family didn't have electricity and running water, she was determined to see the good in everyone and every situation.

"We might have been poor but we didn't know it / We'd heard that word but we didn't know what it meant."

Her diaristic approach to songwriting also gave birth to hits like Jolene – written about a red-headed love rival – and All I Can Do, a heartfelt declaration of love to her husband, Carl Dean.

Funny and authentic, she captured the trials and tribulations of life in a way that was always relatable, even when her stage outfits and her hairstyle remained larger than life.

The feminist message of 9 To 5 was preceded by When Possession Gets Too Strong and Just Because I'm A Woman, which castigated double standards in relationships: "My mistakes are no worse than yours / Just because I'm a woman."

And in an era where women were forced into gendered stereotypes – housewife, temptress, fallen woman, mixed-up girl – she satirised and sent up those roles, playing them to the hilt while emphasising her strength.

"I've always been misunderstood because of how I look," she sang on 2008's Backwood Barbie. "Don't judge me by the cover, cos I'm a real good book."

Words like those inspired generations of women to be who they were, not who the world perceived them as.

And she used her music to unite people, even as much of the country music establishment entrenched itself in conservatism.

In 2002, at the House of Blues in Los Angeles, Parton even replaced the name Jolene with "drag queen" as a crowd of drag performers looked on.

Outside music, her philanthropy gave scholarships to impoverished students and supplied more than 200 million books to young readers.

Significantly, none of the country stars she inspired were ever billed as "the next Dolly Parton" because no-one did it like Dolly. She was unique. Irreplaceable. Unreproducible.

A legend in her lifetime, and now beyond.

articles.title: Rupert Grint to return to Harry Potter in Broadway play Harry Potter and the Cursed Child
articles.text:
Harry Potter star Rupert Grint is to return to the role of Ron Weasley - playing the character as an adult in the spin-off play in New York.

Grint was first cast to play Ron in the original films at the age of 11. Now 38, he will join the cast of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child on Broadway for four months from next February.

The play catches up with Harry, Ron and Hermione as grown-ups, 19 years after the end of the events in the original books and films - with Ron and Hermione now married and sending their daughter to Hogwarts.

"Dusting off the old robes. New York - see you all in February," Grint wrote on Instagram, external.

Last November, he told BBC News he was unlikely to ever "step out" of Ron Weasley's shadow. "I'm fine with that. I think it's great," he said.

In a statement on Wednesday, the British actor said: "Ron Weasley has been a part of me since I was 11 years old and I can't wait to meet him again in this stage of life.

"There is something so full-circle and so special about stepping back into Ron's shoes now when we are both fathers; it is somehow both very familiar and completely new.

"And the joy of being back on Broadway, this time in a role that defined so much of my life is truly exciting."

Grint is the only one of the main three stars from the films to return to their roles, although co-star Tom Felton is currently reprising his role as Draco Malfoy in the same play.

They are not due to appear on stage together, however - Felton will appear until 3 January, with Grint joining on 2 February. He is currently scheduled to appear until 30 May.

articles.title: How Dolly Parton told her life story through six iconic songs
articles.text:
The much-loved US singer-songwriter, actress and philanthropist Dolly Parton, who has died aged 80, was known as the Queen of Country.

Raised in Tennessee, she rose to fame in the late 1960s with hits that bridged country and pop music.

Her songs covered deeply personal themes around growing up poor, love and loss, as well as female empowerment and spirituality.

Following Parton's death, here is a look back at her life through the lens of six iconic songs.

Let's start with Dolly Parton's own personal favourite, her 1971 acoustic country-folk ditty, Coat of Many Colors, external.

The autobiographical track, taken from the album of the same name, tells the heart-stirring tale of how she grew up poor - as one of 12 siblings - but rich in love.

In her book, Songteller: My Life in Lyrics, Parton described it as a "little story" that covers "a world of things", with teachings about bullying, acceptance, love and good parenting.

The lyrics go: "Now I know we had no money, but I was rich as I could be / In my coat of many colors my momma made for me".

The song has been covered by the likes of Shania Twain and Eva Cassidy, and Rolling Stone magazine put it in second place in its list of Parton's top 50 songs, external.

"Had it been the only song she'd ever written, the expression of overwhelming pride and crushing anguish... would have secured her indelible legacy," the US magazine wrote in 2023.

Coat of Many Colors is also the title of Parton's own children's book, and a 2015 TV movie based on her life - starring Alyvia Alyn Lind as the precocious young singer dreaming of fame.

Her mother, Avie Lee Parton, even made her daughter a new patchwork coat to put on display at the museum inside the Dollywood theme park in her home state of Tennessee.

Parton penned many songs about all different aspects of her relationship with her devoted husband Carl Dean, who ran an asphalt paving business in Nashville.

This included the fear that she might lose him, specifically to a red-headed bank clerk who had flirted with him early on in their marriage.

We all know her by now, of course, as the infamous Jolene, external.

With its fast fingerstyle minor riff, the song was nominated for a Grammy in 1974 and gave Parton her second number one single on the Billboard Hot Country Singles chart and her first foray into the main Hot 100 chart (60).

It also showed Parton at her most vulnerable, making it all the more relatable.

Instead of shedding tears or vowing revenge, we hear the protagonist in the song begging the mistress who holds the power to relinquish it.

"She got this terrible crush on my husband," Parton told US media in 2008. "And he just loved going to the bank because she paid him so much attention. It was kinda like a running joke between us - I was saying, 'Hell, you're spending a lot of time at the bank. I don't believe we've got that kind of money.'"

Parton had met Dean outside a laundromat on the first day she arrived in Nashville as an 18-year-old aspiring singer. The pair were married for 60 years, until his death in 2025.

A notoriously private man, he was "a little embarrassed" when she wrote Jolene, Parton said in a 2023 interview with BBC's The One Show, external, adding that "actually, it wasn't as serious [as it sounds]. I was just jealous 'cause she was a beautiful woman and he was just flirting.

"So it gave me a great idea for a song. There's always a Jolene in somebody's life."

She joked that later in life when she saw her, by now, much older husband snoozing in his chair at home, she thought Jolene "can have him now... where's Jolene when you need her?!"

Jolene is her most popular song, having been streamed more than 913 million times on Spotify. Critics from Rolling Stone to the Guardian, external agree it's her best.

Beyoncé gave it a modern rewrite for her 2024 Cowboy Carter, external album, changing the lyrics from: "I'm begging of you, please, don't take my man" to "I'm warning you, don't come for my man."

Despite the romantic sounding title, this 1974 song, external is actually the sound of Parton tenderly asking her musical mentor, Porter Wagoner, to let her go and pursue her solo career.

Parton was 21 when she joined Wagoner's variety TV show. They released a string of duets and toured together, leading fans to think they were an item.

But they had a complicated relationship, with Parton later writing in another book, Star of the Show: My Life on Stage, that she felt Wagoner saw her rise as a "threat".

"I was making my way as an artist, and he was already an established one. It was his show, but I was trying to grow in the business and grow as an artist myself."

On the track we hear her sing: "Bittersweet memories / That is all I'm taking with me".

Rough Trade's music blog, external once described it as being "heartwarming in its sentiment, crushing in its delivery."

Elvis Presley was set to record a cover of the song in 1974, but Parton made the difficult decision to back out of the deal when his manager demanded half of the songwriting rights.

"I said, 'I can't do that'," she told Howard Stern in 2023. "Of course I cried all night about that."

Parton re-recorded I Will Always Love You in 1982 for her starring role in the musical comedy film, The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas.

But arguably the most iconic version comes courtesy of Whitney Houston who can be heard booming it out in another film, 1992's The Bodyguard. Her version remains the biggest-selling US single by a female artist.

Parton said she heard the power ballad version for the first time on the radio, and felt so overwhelmed that she had to pull over to avoid crashing her Cadillac.

Whitney Houston took her "little country song" and made it "so much more", she said.

This defiant anthem of female empowerment, released in 1980, was the most transformative of her career.

Already well established as a singer, 9 To 5, external brought Parton over into the mainstream popular culture.

She wrote the country-tinged southern soul number as the theme tune for the comedy film of the same name, which saw her make her movie debut alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin.

It tells the story of three working women who live out their fantasies of getting even with, and overthrowing, their company's bigot of a boss (played by Dabney Coleman).

The song's distinctive tapping beat at the start is none other than her acrylic nails: "I always play the nails and I'd come up with little things that I would see on the set, like 'I tumble out of bed and I stumble to the kitchen'… And I thought, 'Wow, that sounds like a typewriter,'" she once explained.

Parton won two Grammys for the chart-topping tune, which was also nominated for an Oscar, and later spawned a Broadway musical and a documentary.

A modern day karaoke classic, Parton recorded this hit with fellow US country star Kenny Rogers, external as the lead single for his 1983 album, Eyes That See in the Dark.

The deep love song sold millions of copies and topped both the country and pop charts at the same time.

It was actually written for them by the Bee Gees, intended as a Motown-inspired duet. The Gibb brothers later recorded their own version and performed it live.

Parton and Rogers' rendition, though, remains one of most popular country-pop duets of all time and a classic of the genre.

Their collaboration was "another thing I'm as proud of as anything I ever did in my musical career," she told Smooth Radio, external 40 years on, in 2023.

She added: "You want to do well and keeping up with the likes of Barry [Gibb] and Kenny [Rogers], but I just figure I'll just always be me and do me and that seems to work."

articles.title: Tim Curry: The Rocky Horror Picture Show star dies at 80
articles.text:
English actor Tim Curry, best known for playing the outlandish Frank-N-Furter in film musical The Rocky Horror Picture Show, has died at the age of 80.

Curry first played the role on stage before the film version, which was released in 1975 and has remained a cult favourite.

The actor also played fearsome clown Pennywise in the 1990 TV version of Stephen King's It, and was Long John Silver in 1996's Muppet Treasure Island.

His other films included Annie, The Hunt for Red October, Home Alone 2, Scary Movie 2 and he was nominated for three Tony Awards on Broadway.

Born in Warrington in 1946, Curry's first acting job after university was in the original London production of groundbreaking rock musical Hair in 1968.

In 1973, a fellow cast member, Richard O'Brien, asked Curry to audition for his new musical, and cast him in the role of the flamboyant lingerie-clad "sweet transvestite" Dr Frank-N-Furter.

Curry first put his stamp on the character of the riotous scientist on stage in the upstairs theatre at London's Royal Court in 1973.

The show's popularity snowballed and resulted in a big-screen adaptation, which also starred Susan Sarandon, Barry Bostwick and O'Brien.

It was not an immediate hit at cinemas but became a fan favourite and holds the record for the longest-running theatrical release in film history.

Welsh actor Luke Evans, who played the role in a Broadway revival, called Curry "a force, a bright fierce flame, an exquisite charm".

In a letter he recently wrote to Curry, Evans thanked him for his fearlessness and for "creating something so enduring, and for inspiring generations of actors to be a little braver than they thought they could be".

"Being compared to you has been one of the greatest compliments I've ever received, even though it's a comparison no one could ever hope to live up to," he wrote in the letter.

The official Rocky Horror Picture Show on Broadway account similarly thanked the late actor for "giving the world a little more freedom, a little more fearlessness, and through the tears in our eyes, the courage to BE IT" - a nod to Curry's deliver of the famous line from the musical, "Don't dream it, be it".

A statement from Curry's representatives following his death said: "Across five decades, he moved fluidly between comedy, horror, drama, and music, delighting himself and his legion of fans with his countless dynamic personas."

They added: "Few actors can claim to have left as many distinct fingerprints on pop culture - and though he suffered a debilitating stroke in 2012, he continued adding to his achievements as an artist and, most recently, a writer.

"Though widely known for his inimitable, flamboyant characters and colorful stage performances, his greatest legacies to those who knew him were his curious, expansive mind and generous, gentle heart, both of which remained open and filled with anticipation until his final breath."

American comedy icon Carol Burnett, who shared a clip of Curry's turn as her smarmy brother in Annie alongside Bernadette Peters, wrote on social media that "nobody could play lovable villains better than he could".

US actor Rob Schneider, who played the bell boy to Curry's uppity hotel clerk in Home Alone 2, said that he was "gutted" by Curry's death.

"The sensational character actor, Tim Curry has left the stage," Schneider wrote. "A truly gifted performer of stage and screen, his one eyebrow could say more than most actors entire bodies. I am grateful to have the rare gift of watching him work, he made you better just standing near him."

articles.title: The wit and wisdom of Dolly Parton: 'If you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain'
articles.text:
"I'm not going to limit myself just because people won't accept the fact that I can do something else."

"I actually take my songwriting more serious than anything else I do, so I would say I am a songwriter first."

"You have to search for a long time because I've written a lot of songs. But yes, there are pieces of me, of course, in everything I write."

"I have to write and sing. See, that was my first love, and I have to do that forever, however I have to do it."

"I look totally artificial, but I am totally real, as a writer, as a professional, as a human being. A rhinestone shines just as good as a diamond."

"I always count my blessings, more than I count my money. I don't work for money, never did. It was the art, it was the job. I loved the work. And I've done well, and I'm thankful for it."

"I wanted more than to just be a farmer's daughter, even though I'm proud to be [one]. I just wanted pretty things. I wanted money to buy the things I had always been impressed with as a child. I wanted, I guess, to be a star."

"If I was trying to describe myself to someone that had never seen me before, I would say, 'Calm down. Don't get scared. It's just me. I know I look totally bizarre and artificial, but I'm totally real inside.'"

"I don't like to be like everybody else. I've often made the statement that I would never stoop so low as to be fashionable. That's the easiest thing in the world to do."

"I make jokes about it, but it's the truth that I kind of patterned my look after the town tramp. I didn't know what she was, just this woman who was blond and piled her hair up, wore high heels and tight skirts, and, boy, she was the prettiest thing I'd ever seen. Momma used to say, 'Aw, she's just trash', and I thought, 'That's what I want to be when I grow up. Trash.'"

"I'm pretty sharp. I'm not educated and I'm not that intelligent, but I'm smart. They say somebody's street smart. I feel like if I got intelligence, it's just a country smart."

Journalist: "What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?" Dolly: "The fact that sometimes my mouth is a little too big and a little too open and sounds too much like a sailor."

"They say love isn't about two people gazing into each other's eyes, it is about two people gazing outwards in the same direction. I believe this with all my heart."

"I never really tried to hide myself from anybody. I think that's one of the reasons I'm still around, people feel like they know me."

Speaking more about the book gifting programme for children: "Since I had no kids and my husband was pretty independent, I had freedom. So I think a big part of my success is the fact that I was free to work. And I didn't have children, because I believe that God didn't mean for me to have kids, so everybody's kids could be mine, so I could do things like the Imagination Library."

"I ain't never gonna be old because I ain't got time to be old. I can't stop long enough to grow old. I'm just gonna be the best I can be at whatever age I am."

"When I'm done, I can rest in peace knowing I've done my best. I hope that when my time comes, I'll leave something behind that others can use to lift themselves up."

"When I die, I'll really be getting to live then because I believe that there is a greater place than this".

"I've got transgender people. I've got gays. I've got lesbians. I've got drunks. I've got drug addicts - all within my own family. I know and love them all, and I do not judge."

In a letter to young recipients of books from Dolly Parton's Imagination Library: "You and all of your friends are very special. There is no limit to what you can do or how far you can go."

She continued: "Just remember the lessons my family taught me - dream big dreams; learn everything you can learn; and care for all those who care for you. You do all of these things and you can be anyone you want to be.

articles.title: How Dolly Parton helped the world - from children's books to supporting Covid vaccine
articles.text:
Dolly Parton will not only be remembered for her iconic songs and Southern charm, but also for her philanthropic work.

Throughout her life, she supported communities in need, especially in her home state of Tennessee. She funded medical research that led to one of the first Covid-19 vaccines, donated to wildfire victims and even helped the once-endangered bald eagle, America's national bird.

But it is her Imagination Library - the mainstay of her charity work - that has helped millions of children learn to read by sending out free books.

The programme was inspired by her father who couldn't read or write.

"I think deep down inside, my daddy was prouder of [the library] than he even was of my career," she wrote.

Parton established her non-profit organisation, the Dollywood Foundation, in 1988, to help bolster children's education. Its efforts are practical - like sending out books - and often goes directly to the grass roots, where it can really make a difference, fast.

In the early 90s, Parton said she'd give every seventh and eighth-grade student (ages 12 to 14) in Sevier County, Tennessee, where she grew up, $500 if they graduated high school. They had to have a buddy, to keep each other in check - which in turn made more children graduate.

Sure, it was a bit of a bribe, but it worked - the drop out rate went from 35% to 6%, according to the foundation's website.

"I'm kind of addicted to the feeling of giving," she once said. "Knowing that I'm doing something good for someone else."

Parton was awarded the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy in 2022, which honoured her as "one of the entertainment world's most generous philanthropists".

Dolly Parton was one of 12 children born into a poor family that lived in a one-bedroom cabin in the Smoky Mountains. Her hardworking father, Robert Lee Parton, was a tobacco farmer.

"He was the smartest man I have ever known but I know in my heart his inability to read probably kept him from fulfilling all of his dreams," Dolly wrote.

Inspired by this, the Imagination Library was launched in 1995, with the help of Robert Parton. It sends out free books to children younger than five every month.

The programme was originally set up just for those in Sevier County - but it quickly went national and then global. The Imagination Library now sends books to children across the US, Canada, UK, Ireland and Australia.

According to its website, more than 332.4 million books have been sent out.

For many children who have never owned their own book, it is a special gift just for them.

"It's the fact they get recognised," Parton once said. "They get this little book with their little name on it in the mail, and they feel special... they know that somebody out there is thinking of them."

"That vision she had about books and this understanding of sharing stories was remarkable," Eileen Driver, the chair of the Stokesley Imagination Library in the UK, told the BBC's Radio Tees.

Scottish National Party councillor, Lee Mills - admittedly a superfan from a young age - said when he was elected he set out to bring the Imagination Library to Dundee.

"Dolly's legacy will last with every page turned of a children's book. I will do my utmost best to ensure that this is delivered to every child in Scotland," he told the BBC.

British author Selina Brown, whose book My Rice is Best was one of those selected to be distributed, told the BBC it was quite emotional to see 14,000 copies of her book being packed up, ready to post.

"For my book in particular, the protagonist is black. It helps with representation, it helps with real life situations and having a book that speaks directly to you and speaks to a different world is important."

During Covid, Parton started reading some of the books aloud, in recordings on YouTube for children - many of whom didn't know who she was.

"You mean she sings, too?" exclaimed one boy when he found out, Linda Jinnette Cooper wrote on the library's Facebook page.

In 2020, as the Covid-19 pandemic gripped the world, Parton encouraged people to get vaccinated and donated $1m (£716,000) to the Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, which helped fund the Moderna vaccine.

A portion of the money went towards funding an early stage-trial of the Moderna vaccine, which found it to offer nearly 95% protection against severe Covid-19.

Reimagining her hit song, Jolene, Parton changed the lyrics to "vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, I'm begging of you, please don't hesitate".

She showed herself being injected, saying: "I'm old enough to get it and I'm smart enough to get it."

Parton donated to medical research several times over the years.

A benefit concert in 2007 raised $1m for a new hospital and cancer centre in Sevier County, which includes a Dolly Parton Center for Women's Services.

Ten years later, she released a children's album, I Believe in You, and donated another $1m, this time to Nashville's Monroe Carell Jr. Children's Hospital at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, after her niece was treated for leukaemia there.

She donated yet another $1m to the hospital a few years later, this time to help paediatric infectious disease research.

"I love children," Parton said in a statement at the time. "No child should ever have to suffer, and I'm willing to do my part to try and keep as many of them as I can as healthy and safe as possible."

And earlier this year, the East Tennessee Children's Hospital announced it would be renamed to the Dolly Parton Children's Hospital, after the star partnered with the not-for-profit facility.

Her Dollywood amusement park has a lot more than rollercoasters - it's also home to the largest sanctuary for non-releasable bald eagles in the world.

Managed by the American Eagle Foundation, its rehabilitation and breeding work has won awards and in 2007, the bald eagle was removed from the endangered species list.

In 2022, Parton's charity work to improve education was extended to adults, when it was announced that any Dollywood employee - whether they were seasonal, part-time or full-time, would have 100% of their tuition and books paid for if they furthered their education.

In announcing her death on Tuesday, Parton's team asked fans to donate to the Imagination Library, instead of sending flowers, so that her legacy can continue for many years to come.

"When I'm done, I can rest in peace knowing I've done my best," Parton once said.

"I hope that when my time comes, I'll leave something behind that others can use to lift themselves up."

Additional reporting by Olivia Ireland

articles.title: V&A museum workers to strike in September over pay and conditions
articles.text:
Workers at three Victoria and Albert Museum sites in London will strike next month over pay, health and safety, and working conditions.

Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union members at V&A East Storehouse, V&A East and Young V&A are due to walk out on 4 and 5 September.

Members of Prospect, another trade union, will also walk out in a parallel dispute. Members of the two unions at the three V&A sites will work to rule and withdraw co-operation from 4 September onwards.

A V&A spokesperson said the museum had been negotiating with the unions since February and had met the majority of their demands with "a significantly improved offer".

A PCS ballot registered 95% in favour of industrial action. The union did not say how many workers would be striking.

It called for better pay, a cross-site policy to close public spaces when temperatures reached 30C, and for V&A East Storehouse workers "to drink and carry water at work".

Fran Heathcote, PCS general secretary, said members had given the V&A "every opportunity" to resolve the dispute through negotiation and if management wanted to avoid further disruption, it needed to get around the table "and start negotiating seriously".

Mike Clancy, general secretary of Prospect, said the union was making "very reasonable demands" over pay and working conditions for its members.

The V&A spokesperson said they valued their staff enormously and were committed to providing safe and supportive work environments.

"Our latest pay offer delivers a pay rise well above inflation for all staff, with an average 4.2% pay rise and a 6.9% increase for our lowest-paid colleagues."

They said the V&A had a longstanding commitment to paying at least the London Living Wage.

"All our staff have regular breaks, and access to drinking fountains on each floor is provided at V&A East Storehouse, which has an air-cooling system.

"Extensive heatwave mitigation has also been put in place across our museums."

Visitors are advised to check museum websites for updates on any disruption.

articles.title: Yayoi Kusama, Japanese artist who became a global superstar, dies aged 97
articles.text:
Yayoi Kusama, the Japanese outsider artist who reached superstar status after decades living in a psychiatric hospital, has died aged 97.

Kusama died in a Tokyo hospital on 14 August, her company Yayoi Kusama Inc announced in a statement on Thursday.

“Throughout an extraordinary lifetime devoted entirely to artistic creation, Kusama pursued an internationally acclaimed career as a pioneering avant garde artist whose creative practice encompassed visual art, performance, fiction, and poetry,” the statement read. “She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush, and continued exploration of forever love and eternal soul.”

“We will carry forward Kusama’s wishes and, through art, continue to bring hope and strength for the future to people around the world.”

Instantly recognisable by her bright red bobbed wig, Kusama became known for her psychedelic colour schemes and “infinity mirror room” installations, which helped her find a huge audience in the age of the social media selfie: her 2024 show in Australia was the most popular exhibition in the country’s history. Yet she had pioneered many of her enduring themes as a young artist in the 1960s, before fading into temporary obscurity.

As well as being a sculptor and painter, Kusama put on numerous performance pieces throughout the hippy era that saw her name attached to scandal. She staged “body festivals” with naked performers painted in polka dots and once wrote to US president Richard Nixon offering to sleep with him in return for an end to the Vietnam war. News of such events appalled her conservative family back home.

Kusama was born in Matsumoto, Japan, in 1929, enduring an unhappy childhood at the hands of an abusive mother and philandering father. Her wealthy family managed plant nurseries and Kusama would sit and draw the flowers despite her mother’s frequent attempts to stop her. As a child, Kusama began experiencing hallucinations, in which the flowers would swarm around and talk to her. Her coping mechanism was to draw what she saw.

During the second world war, 13-year-old Kusama was conscripted to produce fabric for Japanese army parachutes. She later studied nihonga, a traditional Japanese style of painting, in Kyoto, but grew frustrated with its limitations. Rejecting her planned future of an arranged marriage and children, Kusama left Japan for New York in 1958. There, she fell in with the artist and theorist Donald Judd and made a breakthrough with her “infinity net” paintings – vast fields of impastoed polka dots that stretched across the canvas. In 1962, she sold her first of these to the artists Frank Stella and Judd for $75. In 2014, her White No 28 sold for $7.1m (£5.7m) at auction, a record at the time for a living female artist.

In 1963, Kusama started making “soft sculptures” – pieces of furniture and other objects, such as ladders, covered with white, fabric-stuffed phallic shapes. They were, she said, her attempt to heal her disgust around sex, which she had been brought up to believe was dirty and shameful.

Despite working loosely within the spheres of pop art and minimalism, Kusama was not embraced by the art world. She always maintained that many of her ideas from this period were appropriated by white male artists, including Andy Warhol, while she was written out of art history.

Kusama’s work was often centred around the infinite and the idea of “self-obliteration”, a concept inspired by the hallucinations that would engulf her. Talking about her 1954 painting Flower (DSPS), she once said: “I was looking at the red flower patterns of the tablecloth on a table, and when I looked up I saw the same pattern covering the ceiling, the windows and the walls, and finally all over the room, my body and the universe. I felt as if I had begun to self-obliterate, to revolve in the infinity of endless time and the absoluteness of space, and be reduced to nothingness.”

At the 1966 Venice Biennale she continued these studies, presenting her infamous Narcissus Garden, a “lake” of 1,500 reflective balls that strived for a sense of mirrored infinity. When Kusama began selling the balls for $2 each under the banner “Your narcissism for sale”, the biennale moved to close the operation down.

Kusama developed a flair for controversy. Her artistic “happenings” were often criticised for being mere shock material, yet their political statements now seem ahead of their time. In 1968, she staged New York’s first “homosexual wedding” in Tribeca and washed a “dirty” Soviet flag outside the United Nations building in protest over the invasion of Czechoslovakia.

By this time Kusama was engaged in a platonic yet obsessive relationship with the outsider artist Joseph Cornell, which continued even after she had left the US to return to Japan. She had been frequently admitted to hospital during her time in New York and when Cornell died in 1972, her mental health deteriorated further, with hallucinations, panic attacks and suicide attempts. In 1977, she checked herself into a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo that offered art therapy courses and provided Kusama with the stability needed to pursue her projects without distraction. She made the decision to live there permanently, working each day from morning until night in her nearby studio.

Although she published several novels during the 1980s, interest in Kusama appeared to have waned almost completely by the start of the 90s. But the recognition that eluded her during her early artistic career finally arrived later in life. In 1993 she created a mirrored room filled with small pumpkin sculptures for the Venice Biennale’s Japanese pavilion and won plaudits for the work. She had first seen a pumpkin with her grandfather when she was 11. When she tried to pick it, it had appeared to start speaking to her, and now it became a recurring motif in works such as All the Eternal Love I Have for the Pumpkins, from 2016.

Kusama’s focus shifted towards installations that built on her 1965 work Infinity Mirror Room: Phalli’s Field. In that piece, hundreds of soft, pink phallic forms were arranged within a mirrored room. Half a century later, such immersive experiences connected with audiences on a global scale, with the coloured lights and brightly painted pumpkins providing perfect Instagram content. It was not without irony that an exhibition of hers at the Hirshhorn Museum in Washington DC in 2017 was temporarily closed after someone damaged an artwork while attempting to take a selfie.

Kusama received retrospectives at the New York’s Museum of Modern Art in 1998, Tate Modern in London in 2012 and Washington DC’s Hirshhorn Museum in 2017. Tickets for her shows sold out swiftly around the world and fans would queue for hours just to be allowed a 30-second experience within her installations.

Despite some critics wondering if she had become the world’s most popular artist, Kusama always believed that her place in history would not be decided by the art establishment.

articles.title: Jeers, walkouts, stage invasions: will Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists trigger British audiences too?
articles.text:
In February, turbulent scenes inside a German theatre made headlines around the globe. During the final act of a play at Schauspielhaus theatre in Bochum, the audience first jeered and whistled at a performer in the role of a far-right politician. An orange lobbed from the auditorium narrowly missed its target; eventually, two spectators climbed on to the stage and tried to wrestle the actor off. News of the incident travelled around the world: it seemed a bizarre throwback to a world in which people were not able to tell the difference between art and real life, like 19th-century Parisians stampeding out of a cinema after watching a train hurtle towards the camera.

For the man who wrote the play, however, it was nothing unusual. “I was not surprised by the reaction,” says Portuguese playwright Tiago Rodrigues. “I was surprised by the fact that it was so surprising for so many people.” He describes the audience’s reaction to his play Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists as “very intense”, but also “typical”.

The play, which visits London’s National Theatre next month, tells the story of a macabre family tradition: once every year, a group of relatives gather over a feast of wild boar and asparagus in the southern Portuguese countryside to kill a fascist they have kidnapped. Their ritual is designed to avenge the real-life murder of Catarina Eufémia, a harvester in revolt who was killed at the hands of the Salazar regime’s police force in 1954. But this year the family member tasked with the execution voices some doubts about the ritual’s righteousness, and things go awry: in the play’s last half hour, the freed fascist gives a victory speech that is uninterrupted by the rest of the cast. Ever since its September 2020 premiere in Guimarães, audiences have stepped in to intervene.

In Portugal, spectators chanted Grândola, Vila Morena, José Afonso’s song of the 1974 Carnation revolution, to drown out the actor’s words. In Italy, they sang anti-fascist resistance anthem Bella Ciao. In Austria, spectators stood up and walked out. There were attempts to storm the stage and hit the actor impersonating the fascist politician at performances in Lisbon, Paris, Marseille and in Montreal. In other places, it was the far right that expressed its indignation: the Rome premiere of Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists was met with protests from the local branch prime minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party, which asked for the play to be removed from the programme.

“We always get these reactions, whether we’re in Switzerland or in Norway,” Rodrigues says, matter-of-factly. “In around 200 performances, we’ve had perhaps a handful of shows where the audience just listened to the final speech in silence.”

What is it about his play that has made it a 21st-century equivalent of Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring, triggering mini-riots wherever it is shown? One answer may be that Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists is essentially two plays in one, each of which annuls the answers offered by the other: an anti-fascist play that asks difficult questions of both liberal and militant anti-fascists.

For the first two hours, Rodrigues’s play is a reflection on what the philosopher Karl Popper called the “paradox of tolerance”: to preserve an open and tolerant society, must we be intolerant towards those who advocate intolerance? Or does our society cease to be a tolerant one when we do so? The second question carries particular weight in Rodrigues’s staging, for the anti-fascist tradition that the family at the heart of the play represents is one that comes across as self-absorbed, self-regarding and, in its own way, reactionary. “Our family killed fascists during the dictatorship, we killed fascists during the democracy and will continue to kill fascists,” says one of the characters, Pedro. “You shouldn’t ask yourself ‘Why?’ or ‘Why also me?’. The real ‘why’ is in the ‘how’. There’s a method, a ritual, a tradition, a beauty.”

It’s hard not to side with Sara, the young woman who has been chosen to kill her first fascist this year but instead of duty feels only doubt. Is killing not like imposing a dictatorship, she asks: “Death, where you don’t think, don’t argue, where you can’t change your mind, is that not the greatest dictatorship of all?” And if the end supposedly justifies the means, why has their ritual not managed to fend off fascism for good (in the play, the extreme right has recently gained power over Portugal again)? “Why don’t we have a revolution, a coup d’état, a guerrilla campaign, a war? Why don’t we kill all the fascists once and for all and get this thing sorted?”

Rodrigues, who has been artistic director of the D’Avignon theatre festival since 2022, does not hide his sympathies with Sara’s inner conflict. “My own views are quite simple,” he says. “I consider the far right an enemy that has to be fought, but we should fight them in a democratic way, and if that doesn’t work, you keep on playing it democratic. I think most of the audience usually position themselves in a similar way: they feel Sara is right.

“Nevertheless, there have been moments in history where violence was considered a legitimate response to fascism. Where I live today, in the south of France, I don’t think it’s controversial to say that armed resistance was a legitimate answer to the Nazi occupation.”

With the family of anti-fascists unable to come to a collective decision on how to address their problem, the fascist politician is freed and gives a victory speech straight out of the modern far right’s rulebook, decrying the dictatorship of “minorities” over “the people”, the biased mainstream media, the intolerant liberal left. If you overthink your anti-fascism, Rodrigues seems to be saying in response to the first part of the play, this is what you get.

The playwright says he wrote the final monologue during the rehearsals. “We had this problem: how do we finish? If Sara’s side won, it would be very didactic and politically correct. And I realised the victory of the far right would be the most troubling, the most dystopian and also the most thought-provoking.” His own cast’s response to the ending foreshadowed the reactions the play has received around the globe. “Some people felt sick, others were in tears and left the room or thought about quitting the project altogether. There were a lot of debates about whether we have the right to put such a speech on stage today.”

He condemns those who have tried to assault members of his cast, but says it’s not for him to judge spectators shouting down a fascist speech: “It’s not something that we find to be a mistake.” Some viewers, he believes, feel the play is inviting them to react in a visceral way: “They feel they have to show emotion because the actor is addressing them, and if they don’t protest they are accomplices of his speech. For them, it’s a kind of game they’ve been invited to play.”

In other cases, he suggests, the outrage may also cloak a deeper feeling of helplessness: “The audience have spent two hours following a complex debate and worked out their own position within it, and suddenly that choice is not there any more. That’s very disturbing. Some of the same people who agreed most strongly with Sara that the left should not use violence are the loudest to scream ‘kill him’ at the end of the play.”

Rodrigues decided to tackle the question of how societies can protect themselves from fascism after André Ventura, the founder of anti-immigration party Chega, in 2019 became the first far-right politician to be elected as a member of Portugal’s parliament since the end of the Salazar regime. Until that point, the Iberian country had looked immune to the brand of rightwing populism that was rattling most countries in Europe.

“I remember when I mentioned in rehearsals that the story would be about a victory for the far right in 2028. Everybody laughed: yeah, that’s never going to happen, eight years is too short. And I agreed with it. My defence was that we needed to exaggerate to focus the audience’s mind.” Today, Chega is the second largest party in Portuguese politics; earlier this year, Ventura came second in a rare runoff vote for the presidency.

“As a playwright, you are sometimes dystopian because you don’t want to be prophetic,” he adds. “Unfortunately, reality keeps making this piece more relevant.”
